## The Winged

The Winged was a fallen planetar that dwelled on the Prime Material plane, in the nation of Thay on Toril during the late 14 century DR. She was once a servant of Torm, the God of Duty, before her downfall.

Personality
The Winged was a guarded and personal individual who seldom spoke to anyone other than Dennaton, the operator of a gladiatorial arena in Thay, and members of her mercenary company, the Planar Hunters. She always ensured she was paid in full, and exactly on time according to her schedule.

Possessions
Among her other possessions, the Winged wore a single, unique gauntlet that granted her exceptional power in combat. The powerful armored glove could be worn by no one else but her.

Relationships
The Winged led the mercenaries known as the Planar Hunters. Among its members were the admaantine golem Bannor Kaxazel, an efreeti by the name of Dormamus, the bard Joker, the Red Wizard Pol Pyrrus, and a fire salamander called Thassk Kun.

By all appearances, the Winged and her mercenaries worked under the employ of Dennaton. In truth, they were employed by Szass Tam, the Thayan zulkir of necromancy, during his campaign against his rival Aznar Thrul.

Activities
For some time during her existence, the Winged fought as a champion in the Blood War. It was not clear if she fought for the baatezu of the Nine Hells, or somehow aligned herself with the demons of the Abyss.

During her time on Toril, the Winged and the other Hunters served Dennaton by capturing powerful combatants and fearsome beasts and perilous entities that would serve as gladiators in Dennaton's arena. They also acted as enforcers, to ensure the fighters remained subservient between their matches. Among the powers subdued by the Winged and her mercenaries were illithids, fiends from the lower planes, the dragon Yllaxxia and her offspring, and even two children of the god Bhaal, Enegar and Kastulor.

History
Before her fall, the Winged was a servant of the Faerûnian god Torm, who resided within Mount Celestia.

Circa the, The Winged and the Planar Hunters were dispatched by Dennaton to abduct the Champion of Baeloth's Pit after their victory in the Black Pits within the Underdark. The Champion was one of many combatants selected to bolster the popularity of Dennaton's arena.

When the group known as Raskilov's Ragers attempted to rebel against Dennaton, The Winged dispatched them with a single comet.

Some time later, Dennation pitted the Champion of Baeloth's Pit against a squad of fallen astral and monadic devas led by Ariziel.They held a particular and personal hatred for the Winged.

When the Winged and the Hunters were ordered to gather a tarrasque to fight in the arena, and Dennaton remained distracted with other fights, the Champion of Baeloth's Pit orchestrated an uprising of their own. The Winged and the Hunters proved unsuccessful, but managed to survive the encounter. The fallen planeter and her allies and were summoned back to the arena to combat the Champion and other rebellious slaves.

## The Final Sacrifice of the Moon Daughter

The Final Sacrifice of the Moon Daughter was a Sharran text, penned before the 15 century DR.

Content
The scroll was a prophecy or more of an instruction regarding a powerful sacred spear of Shar's faith. The weapon was said to had been wielded by the goddess herself, then placed in the Silent Library by the elders of the Gauntlet of Shar – a hidden Sharran temple complex under the town of Reithwin in the Western Heartlands. The spear would one day be wielded by Shar's chosen champion to perform the final sacrifice of the Nightsong and bring grief to the Moonmaiden. The text warned even true believers away from trying to use the spear, as in their hands the weapon would have no magic, and all they could do was guard it for the prophesied wielder.

## Thrusk

Thrusk was a hardy wild grass often used for making infusions.

Description
Thrusk grew in tufts. It had roots that ran deep, making it very hardy and resistant to droughts and heatwaves.

Usage
An infusion was commonly made from its roots and leaves. The infusion had a number of properties, being bitter but giving a feeling of warmth to the chest, clearing foul tastes from the mouth, and quickly eliminating any headache not due to a severe head-wound. It was popular amongst caravan drivers for those properties.

The flavor the root itself gave to the infusion was bitter and ropy, akin to licorice. It was an acquired taste, and even for cattle it was only sustenance grazing, as they would prefer to graze on just about anything else given a choice.

Dipping currant-studded hardbread in thrusk made a meal known as daybreak-swallow.

History
Thrusk was drunk in Orthil Voldovan's caravan during its passage from Scornubel to Waterdeep late in the .

## The Prioress

The woman only known as the Prioress was a High Priestess of Umberlee, the High Prioress of the Priory of the Depths on the Sword Coast North, and a one-time member of the Kraken Society in the late 14 century DR.

Description
The Prioress was a stunningly beautiful aquatic elf with blue eyes, blue skin, slicked-back green hair, and a powerful, self-important attitude.

Possessions
The Prioress wore a golden circlet on her head and had a powerful ring of divine power on her finger.

History
The Prioress joined the Kraken Society long before the . However, that affiliation came to an end after a betrayal by one of the Society's members – a High Captains of Luskan. That High Captain requested the aid of The Prioress' divine magic to aid him in a plan that would benefit Luskan greatly. Luskar saw an opportunity in the coastal roads being dangerous and unguarded following the Shadow War between the King of Shadows and Neverwinter. The port town of Port Llast lost much of its Neverwintran garrison, making it vulnerable to the Luskan who sought to claim it. The High Captains of Luskan sent The Platinum Pride, seizing Port Llast with no bloodshed. Neverwinter, unable to send its troops to Port Llast by land due to dangers and delays, sent it by the sea. This was where The Prioress came into play. She used Umberlee's divine magic to shield Port Llast from Lord Nasher Alagondar's ship. Luskar planned on the locals accepting the new government under the false pretense of there being no bloodshed.

When the deed was done, Luskar refused to pay the Prioress for her services. Seething with anger over the betrayal, she arose the storms, battering the Luskar ships, preventing northern reinforcements, and trapping the The Platinum Pride. She demanded what was due to be paid. Soon after, a group of adventurers that worked with merchant Sa'Sani arrived at Port Llast by land. They met with the Luskar, who asked for aid against the "mad" priestess who had already killed an envoy – a Luskar official named Khralver Irilingstar‎.

It was unrecorded how the adventurers dealt with The Prioress after braving the challenges of the Priory of the Depths. Some believed that the adventurers quelled Umberlee's wrath with gold. The Prioress demanded 6,000 gp – a fee to stop the storms and offered her aid in destroying The Platinum Pride and helping the adventurers in throwing the Luskar out of Port Llast for a tithe of additional 4,000 gold pieces. By other accords, The Prioress was slain by the Luskar command.

## The House on Drench Lane and Other Stories

The House on Drench Lane and Other Stories was a collection of short stories penned by the Sisters Macabre sometime before the late 15 century DR.

Contents
The book collected several stories, with the tale titled The House on Drench Lane being its flagship work. The story told of a woman who had unnerving dreams of her neighbor standing outside naked in the rain. The woman's vivid dreams became reality when, one rainy day, she looked out of the window and saw the entire community outside, naked in the rain. She witnessed their familiar faces with the blank stares of stuffed animals, all looking at her, calling to come out. Despite being terrified, something alluring was in their calls. When she stepped outside, the nude community stripped her naked, wet and cold, and gave the woman to her neighbor, who smiled at her with an unnerving smile. And then the woman suddenly woke up, everything being seemingly ordinary. But several tendays later, she discovered she was pregnant and was gripped by terror and paranoia. She unsuccessfully tried to end the pregnancy and, in the end, was left with just terror and dread.

History
The House on Drench Lane and Other Stories was published sometime in or before the . One copy of the book was left in the Lower City Graveyard of Baldur's Gate in 1492 DR.

## The Singing Lute

The Singing Lute was a tavern and an eatery located in the Lower City of Baldur's Gate, run by the half-orc bartenders and proprietors Tender Henk and Tender Honk circa 1492 DR.

Location
The Singing Lute stood on the waterfront in The Steeps, offering a scenic view of the Gray Harbor and the Counting House to the east, rising above the water and Flymm Cargo warehouse to the west.

Structure

The tavern was a small building of three floors. The main entrance was located on the second floor, with the first floor taken by the kitchens and the third – by a dining balcony. The main and the first floors had terraces open to customers with seating and tables. The taproom propped was a small bar and several seating spaces with a dumbwaiter connected to the kitchen.

Services
During the day, the Singing Lute offered drinks and opened its kitchens in the evening for dining. Some of the foods prepared included Baldurian seafood stew, grilled rothé ribs, pumpkin stew, and gruel. As the drinks selection went, The Singing Lute offered local brews, beer, wine, tea, and water. However, ordering things off the menu did not guarantee the customers actually got what they ordered due to Tender Henk's "charming" service and personality. In cases where Henk could not provide the service, Tender Honk would fill in for him.

History
By the late 15 century DR, the Hlath patriar family owned the Singing Lute, with Tenders Henk and Honk running the establishment.

## Throckyl

Jandur was a War Wizard of Cormyr in the late 14 century DR.

History
At some point after spring started in the, the Red Wizard Harnrim Starangh assaulted the armory of the sanctum where Vangerdahast dwelt after his retirement as Royal Mage of Cormyr. In doing so, he slew three mages: one with a slaying-snake spell, another by twisting his shielding magic against himself into a paralyzing field, and a third with staeradder poison. He fled after using a spell that burned out all recollections from their minds, preventing their dead bodies from responding to any questioning.

Darthym reported Jandur as dead to the War Wizard Huldyl Rauthur, a fellow War Wizard working in the sanctum.

In particular, Darthym noted that Throckyl had been blown apart, and his head was separated from the rest of his body. As the man bitten by a snake was not decapitated by any spells, Throckyl must've been one of the two guardians of the inner sanctum, strongly implying that Harnrim Starangh's spell to burn away memories could also cause bodily destruction in some cases.

## The Apprentice's Companion

The Apprentice's Companion was a set of instructional book for the novice mages that consisted of at least four tomes, all published sometime before the late 15 century DR.

Content
Book the First
Volume I of The Apprentice's Companion focused on the nature of magic and its absence in the dead magic zones. The tome discussed historical examples when the magic was unreliable, such as the Time of Troubles, during which the Weave was torn apart and reconstructed. These events left scars in the Weave – dead magic zones that rendered all spells unusable and all enchantments non-functional.

Book the Second
Volume II focused on summoning through magic and its uncountable uses. The tome's author expressed their personal preference in using summoning to conjure forth scouts and cannon fodder in battle. As such, the author warned students not to grow attached to summoned creatures as it claimed they were not real, in form, but mere constructs of the Weave. Despite the book's text, that was, in fact, not true for all summoning magics.

Book the Third
Volume III was dedicated to enchanted items as a source of substantial power and a great aid in developing a wizard's skills. The tome discussed all types of magical amulets, rings, and armor and stated that a single item could very well be the difference between life and death.

Book the Fourth
Volume IV of The Apprentice's Companion focused on various practical spell applications that did not involve combat. Examples included the use of faerie fire or see invisibility to see magically concealed traps, spells like fly and gaseous form could allow the mage to bypass glyphs, and lastly, counterspell could be used to negate harmful effects of some magical traps.

Book the Fifth
Volume V was titled The Particulars of a Single-Entity Plane and was dedicated to various pocket planes, such as a djinni's lamp or Magira's chest. Such miniature planes were created to hold a single entity at a time and could be used to trap a creature until another willing or unwilling creature entered the plane and replaced its previous inhabitant. Such planes collapsed immediately if no creature was inhabiting them.

History
In the, several copies of The Apprentice's Companion tomes were stored and sold by Tolna Tome-Monger of the Sorcerous Sundries, a  magic shop in the city of Baldur's Gate.

## Thauvas Zlorn

Thauvas Zlorn, also known as Khornadar of Westgate, was a Red Wizard of Thay active during the late 14 century DR. He was a liaison with the Rightful Conspiracy of Cormyr.

Description
In his disguise as Khornadar, he was tall, with a thin spike-shaped beard.

Abilities
He was capable of using magic to disguise himself, and claimed to have a ward against being magically eavesdropped on, which included some of his surroundings. One of his spells allowed him to sift the thoughts of other people near him. Another of his spells was an offensive flame of some kind.

Relationships
He was a fellow of Naerzil, and served another, unseen mage.

History
Elminster Aumar made the acquaintance of Thauvas Zlorn without him knowing, while the latter was a minor mage of Thay, around the year . Later, in the early spring of the, Elminster disguised himself and infiltrated the Righful Conspiracy, where he met Thauvas Zlorn in his disguise as Khornadar of Westgate. The latter tried to magically pry into the mind of Elminster, but saw nothing of import; during their conversation, he mentioned his intention to call upon the Society of Stalwart Venturers to retrieve lost magic.

Elminster later held up Thauvas as the meeting was raided by the War Wizards of Cormyr, intending to question the man. After a brief magical struggle, Elminster captured him. He admitted to the intention to use the Society of Stalwart Venturers in the aftermath of a successful conspiracy. His interrogation was cut short by the arrival of Narnra Shalace, a Waterdhavian thief, who'd followed Elminster into the meeting, and then ran into him again while escaping the approaching War Wizards. Elminster used much magic to breach his mind.

He was later released as reinforcements came for the Red Wizards; on the arrival of his fellow Red Wizard, Naerzil, he pretended to take control, ordering Naerzil to take everyone prisoner. When Naerzil said Thauvas's own survival depended on a later decision by their superiors, Thauvas spoke with a voice different from his own, and attacked him suicidally, using a spell that echoed Elminster's movements a moment prior. This strongly implied Elminster was controlling him. Thauvas was killed in the attack.

## Those Who Sleep Below

Those Who Sleep Below were a group of mysterious and malevolent entities that dwelled in the deep, sunless reaches of the Trench of Lopok in the Inner Sea. They were imprisoned within those depths, ever diligently being watched over by the Triton Protectorates of the Inner Sea, who prevented anyone from accessing the Trench. The tritons were very unforthcoming on the matter, admitting only that they watched against "Those Who Sleep Below" and that their guardianship was some sacred duty. What exactly they were was a mystery to the mortals, with some believing them to be deities, but in actuality they were obyrith lords.

Notable Members
 Dagon, the one known member of Those Who Sleep Below and the eldest among them.

Worship
Many among the kuo-toa and morkoth believed these entities to be the dark gods of their ancient myths. The early morkoth theocracies in particular believed their gods to be asleep within the Trench of Lopok and that only fervent prayer could one day awaken them. Outside of these beliefs, some legends claimed that the Trench of Lopok was allegedly where both races arose.

They were directly served and worshiped by some krakens and morkoths.

History
In, Kyron the deposed king of Thalorlyn along with his exiled loyalists sought to create a new center of power for himself. Having been driven mad years ago by the whispers of Dagon, he and his loyalists constructed the temple of Vynagyr along the slopes of the Nalaan Plateau and dedicated it to Those Who Sleep Below.In the original text the temple is referred to as being dedicated to "long forgotten evil powers". With Dagon retconned in Grand History of the Realms as a member of Those Who Sleep Below and as the reason behind Kyron's madness, it retroactively suggests that the temple is dedicated to them.

Sometime in the, Those Who Sleep Below commanded their devout kraken servant Qol'in'taroq, along with his morkoth ally Vlantir, to take over the abandoned city of Voalidru for unknown reasons. They only specified that they wished to prevent Voalidru's former merfolk citizenry from ever reclaiming it and its many treasures.

## Thalorlyn

Thalorlyn, also referred to as the First Kingdom of Hmur or the First Thalorlyn, was a kingdom within the Aryselmalyr Empire beneath the Sea of Fallen Stars. It broke away during the Third Serôs War, passing itself off as independent, but was actually a puppet state of Aryselmalyr.

History
In, the Aryselmalyr Empire ignites the Third Serôs War by lashing out against minor raids from aquatic ogres and koalinths. Four years later, in, merfolk within Thalorlyn began rebelling against Aryselmalyr over the oppressive violence that was occurring in the Third Serôs War.

Aryselmalyr's ruler, Coronal Essyl Merynth, secretly appropriates the rebellion by supporting a traitorous merfolk by the name of Kyron, who like him had succumbed to the maddening whispers of Dagon. With the Coronal's influence Kyron slowly rose to a position of leadership among the rebellious merfolk, all the while passing military secrets back to his benefactor.

Two years later, Thalorlyn itself to be independent and claimed the city of Myth Nantar for itself. Under the rule of King Kyron, the Dukars of Myth Nantar would suffer. Rebellions would slowly arise against Thalorlyn's new king. The Aryselmalyr Empire would viciously crack down on this, killing an estimated thirty percent of the merfolk in Serôs.

In, Coronal Essyl had an expedition dispatched to the mysterious Trench of Lopok. His agents would return to him later that same year with a trio of fiendish krakens, fellow servants of Dagon that were willing to ally themselves with the mad rulers, along with a powerful artifact that they forged called the Emerald Eye. Essyl would gift this artifact to Kyron so as to ensure the mad King's loyalty.

In  the various merrows and koalinths of Serôs decided to combine their forces, forming the Horde of the Bloodtide, but this consolidated front continued to be no match against the combined forces of Aryselmalyr and Thalorlyn. That same year a group of spies discovered that the corrupt rulers' secret alliance with the krakens for further power. This revelation led to the formation of a rebel group known as the Republic of Tivaan. Despite the power of their kraken allies and the Emerald Eye, Tivaan managed to depose Kyron and his loyalists a year later, casting them out from the Hmur Plateau and becoming its successor state.

## Thalvan

Thalvan was a merfolk kingdom in Serôs, the realms beneath the Sea of Fallen Stars.

History
In, a massive horde of merrows and koalinths invaded the Hmur Plateau, igniting what would become known as the Fourth Serôs War. Their numbers too great to be overcome, they overran the Plateau and brought about the fall of the Republic of Tivaan. Feeling desperation, a mermaid stole a powerful artifact known as the Emerald Eye of Kyron from one of the towers of the Dukars of Myth Nantar, believing it could drive away the invaders. However, she became corrupted by the Emerald Eye, taken over by what some believed to be the spirit of its original owner contained within the artifact, the Mad King Kyron of Thalorlyn.

With her mind corrupted by the Emerald Eye, the mermaid imposed herself upon the invaders. She proclaimed them to be the Second Kingdom of Kyron and became their leader in a continued conquest of the Hmur Plateau. The war would eventually come to an end in, with the possessed mermaid killed and the Emerald Eye taken back into the custody of the Dukars. The mermaid's body would be buried in the Plains of Duna, subsequently renamed the Haunted Plains, and the Kingdom of Thalvan would be founded by King Darmox as the successor to the Republic of Tivaan.It is never stated within either of the primary sources, Sea of Fallen Stars and Grand History of the Realms, what the "Second Kingdom of Kyron" was. In its summary of the Serôs Wars on page 153, Sea of Fallen Stars states that the Fourth Serôs War's belligerents were the "Second Kingdom of Kyron vs. koalinth and merrow hordes." This would seem to imply that the Republic of Tivaan was this "Second Kingdom of Kyron", however, it seems unlikely that the republic that rebelled against Kyron's rule would take such a name for themselves and is contradicted by the text on the two cited pages stating that the destruction of the Second Kingdom of Kyron adversely affected the Serôsian population of koalinths—if koalinths were in opposition to this Second Kingdom, then its destruction would logically be advantageous to them. This leaves the conclusion that the "Second Kingdom of Kyron" must refer to the collective forces under the mermaid corrupted by the Emerald Eye and the spirit of King Kyron within it.

The Aryselmalyr Empire, having over the past century subjugated the merfolk of Serôs under the reign of Coronal Essyl Merynth, promised Thalvan protection under its new leader, the kindly Coronal Vaeqiis.

## Therapeutics

Therapeutics was a book of research into divination through oneiromancy, written by Margritt Oji sometime before the late 14 century DR.

Content
Margritt Oji's work discussed the writer and researcher's attempts to trigger hallucinations through means that included certain types of incense. However, after numerous unsuccessful attempts to trigger dreams and visions, the oneiromancer in question resorted to taking an undisclosed substance recommended by her own clients. The woman refused to reveal the name of the substance, but it was a fruitful attempt. The oneiromancer's dreams ended up being captured in a painting on a nearby canvas, as intended.

The image was a stance one, depicting a different world, possibly Earth or Eberron, or another similarly technologically advanced crystal sphere. The painting showed massive flying vehicles with what appeared to be some sort of windmills attached to their sides, like wings, and large wheeled locomotives that moved along the rails, with a single humanoid automaton waiving at the painting's observers.

History
A copy of Therapeutics ended up in the House of Healing in the town of Reithwin, deposited there before the settlement was consumed by the shadow-cursed Lands sometime before the . More copies could be found in the city of Baldur's Gate in the .

## Thayan bombard

Thayan bombards, also rendered as Thayvian bombards, were mystical bombards developed by the Red Wizards of Thay. Originally developed as a static defense, but later occasionally put to use on naval vessels, these rare siege engines were considered to be wonders of the 14 century DR.

Description
Much like a standard bombard, these weapons were made from cast iron, but were held together by magic. They were built in two sizes, light and heavy variant. The light variant weighed, while the heavy variant ranged in weight from . The heavy variant was comparably far larger than any standard bombard, with some describing the hulking immobile sentries as being larger than any manor house in the city of Waterdeep.The Dungeon magazine adventure "Operation Manta Ray" features Thayan bombards and states their dimensions on page 52. Though not stated in the text to be the "heavy" variant, the bombards in the adventure can be surmised as being such based on the targeting range given for them. The dimensions in the adventure for a "heavy Thayan bombard" are stated to be a length of  and a diameter of, which are far smaller than being "larger than a Waterdhavian manor house". They required either winches or giants in order to move them.

Weaponology
Thayan bombards required a crew of four to two human-sized individuals to operate them, though a particularly gifted bombardier could potentially operate one single-handedly.

The effective range of these weapons varied between their light and heavy variant. Light bombards had an effective range of, while heavy bombards had a minimum range of  and a maximum range of . Hampered by its immense size, the heavy Thayan bombard had a comparably awful accuracy, but that was made up for with its devastating power. It was incapable of being lowered to aim at anything closer than, while attempts to shoot them at targets further than  found that their projectiles fell long before reaching the desired target. Though the pirates of Dragonisle observed over time that it was technically possible to hit targets from greater distances, so long as they did fired their hollow spheres without any of the accompanying fire-fluid.

Unlike standard bombards, Thayan bombards did not rely upon smokepowder and instead used their own mysterious powder, possibly their own variant on the substance.In Pirates of the Fallen Stars (1992) it stated that a contingent of Gondar clerics were working to "...determine whether the bombards can be used with Lantanna smoke powder, breaking Thay's monopoly on the precious powder used to fire these weapons." This could be interpreted to mean that Thayan bombards use their own proprietary powder instead of smokepowder. However, in the earlier published Forgotten Realms Adventures (1990) they are stated to be smokepowder weapons. This discrepancy between sources could mean either that (1) the earlier source is mistaken, or (2) that the bombards operate on some sort of "Thayan smokepowder", which would explain the choice to specify that the Gondar clergy were trying to determine if they could use "Lantanna smokepowder". The exact nature of how the bombards functioned and their propulsion were both a mystery to those outside of the Red Wizards, mysteries that were compounded by magic the Red Wizards placed over them to further conceal these trade secrets.

Ammunition
In addition to the normal "stone shot" typically fired by bombards, Thayan bombards fired magical bombs. The design of bomb used for much of the 14 century DR were large, hollow stone spheres, filled with a mysterious fluid. This liquid was flammable, alchemical in nature, and known only as "fire-fluid". This fluid would ignite upon firing, becoming a blazing sphere of blue fire that exploded in a burst akin to a fireball. However, these bombs could be inadvertently set off. Because of this precautions were often taken with storing them. According to some accounts, a single one of these "fire bombs" was powerful enough to sink a warship.

Development of other types of magical bombs, ones that could produce a greater variety of dangerous or noxious spell-like effects, began in 1349 DR. Experiments with these would be conducted for the next two decades, until finally they were deemed ready to be mass produced on the plateau of Thaymount (a place secure from outsiders), finally seeing widespread deployment in the early 1370's DR. These later bombs were thick spheres of glass, measuring  in diameter and weighing . Each bomb type had a distinct appearance, reflective of its effect. These effects were triggered and centered upon their point of impact, but for most bombs their effect would only activate if launched from a Thayan bombard. Some of the most common bomb varieties included the following:
Cloudkill bomb A bomb that imitated the effects of the spell cloudkill, though the noxious cloud created could not be moved. A bilious green liquid was visible within them. They had a market value of 1,125 gp.
Death bomb A bomb that imitated the effects of the spell circle of death. These bombs had a black hue, were covered in sinister blue runes, and were cold to the touch. They had a market value of 1,650 gp.
Fireball bomb The most common of bombs, these imitated the effects of the spell fireball. They were warm to the touch and emanated a dull red glow. They were available in three sizes, each having a higher intensity of damage than the last. The three variants of fireball bombs had market values of 375 gp, 450 gp, and 750 gp.
Snowball swarm bomb A bomb that imitated the effects of the spell Snilloc's snowball swarm. These bombs had a blue hue and were covered in frost. They had a market value of 250 gp.
Stinking cloud bomb A bomb that imitated the effects of the spell stinking cloud. A sickly yellow liquid was visible within these bombs. They had a market value of 375 gp.

History
Development on the Thayan bombard began after Thayan spies reported upon the testing of standard bombards that was being conducted on the island nation of Lantan, the first recorded instance of which occurred in, as the Red Wizards declared it was necessary for Thay to command such armaments themselves. The first experiments were conducted in 1312 DR. These experiments were quite disastrous, shredding some poor Red Wizards into little bits. The first successful experiment would be achieved in the .

The first offensive use of a Thayan bombard occurred in the, against a group of living targets that Red Wizards had surrounded. This group was chosen as the Red Wizards were certain that they had no chance of escaping and it was considered critical that the weapon remained a secret.

In the, development began on a new variety of ammunition, glass bombs that could mimic spell effects other than simply fireball. Over the two decades that followed experiments would be conducted, first upon inanimate targets within Thay and later upon living targets along the nation's border with Mulhorand, such as brigands.

Sometime long before 1356 DR,It is not known exactly when the pirates of the Pirate Isles obtained their Thayan bombards, but all early sources repeat the fact that it happened "a long time ago". With the first Forgotten Realms Campaign Set being our earliest source, it had to have occurred before the year 1356 DR. the pirates of the Pirate Isles somehow obtained eight Thayan bombards,Nor is it known exactly how the pirates of the Pirate Isles got their hands on Thayan bombards, considering that the Red Wizards are very defensive of their inventions. For example, on page 24 of Dreams of the Red Wizards one of the rules of the Red Wizards is stated to be that, "...no enchanted item that has military usefulness may be sold outside the country or to a representative of some power outside the country." making them the only entities outside of Thay to possess those wondrous weapons. They stationed batteries on two of the fortresses that stood on Dragonisle, four for each, making the central harbors of their main base incredibly well defended from outside attackers. On the Citadel of Immurk's Hold each of these bombards were sat atop a free turning base, marked with 360 degree marks, and had a hand-screw mechanism that allowed them to be elevated from 45 to 85 degree angles. The hold's pirates ran daily drills to ensure their teams of human signal flag wavers and ogre bombardiers were quite efficient.

However, this great defensive power for the Pirate Isles came at a great cost, for the Thayan bombards were reliant upon the fire-fluid  and precious powder needed to fire these weapons. The pirates purchased both from the tharchioness of Bezantur, Mari Agneh, who parted with both precious substances at a high price. Around 1359 DR, a small contingent of Gondar clerics were on Dragonisle, working with the pirates to discover if it was possible for the bombards to utilize Lantanna's smokepowder in place of the secret powder the bombards were designed to use. This was all done in secrecy, for the Thayans highly valued the monopoly they had on the substances needed to use their bombards and would consider the pirates to be enemies if they were to find out about this treachery.

Up until the 1360's DR, the Thayans themselves rarely utilized the Thayan bombards outside of their own nation. This was due to a combination of their extreme value, the great effort that was required to transport them, and the Red Wizards' desire to keep them a secret. The Thayan bombard would finally see battlefield usage in the 1360's DR, during Thay's campaigns against the nation of Rashemen. With the bombards Thayans managed to damage a wood man so severely that it was forced to retreat. However, the Thayan bombards were later overrun by Rashemaar berserkers, forcing the Thayans to retreat. From that day forward, Thayan bombards would see no further use in the nation's campaigns against Rashemen.

Within Thay itself, dozens of Thayan bombards were stationed on the island tharch of Alaor, which housed the nation's main naval base as well as extensive shipbuilding and repair facilities. And whilst standard bombards were rarely ever utilized on ships, due to their lack of gun-carriages and destructive force sending most styles of ship rolling from side-to-side, the Thayans managed to circumvent this by specially designing ships that could handle them.

The first such ship was the Red Scourge, an impressive warship constructed of enameled red iron and magic. It was outfitted with twenty four light bombards, twelve on each side. A Red Wizard was required to be stationed on the ship at all times in order to supervise the use of the bombards and command their bombardiers. For the sake of safety, the ship's five hundred bombs were kept within iron lockers that were enspelled with an effect equivalent to a ring of fire resistance. The Red Scourge continued to be in action by 1372 DR, but by then the Thayan navy had expanded, developing over a dozen dromonds that were each capable of being outfitted with a pair of light Thayan bombards.

## The Good, the Undead, and the Ugly

The Good, the Undead, and the Ugly is a one round adventure module set in the Living City organized play program. It was published in March 2001, and is Part III of the Flight of Arrows series. It intended for adventurers of 3-12 levels.

Synopsis
After the Zhentarim splinter dissident group – the Flight of Arrows, was granted asylum by the Lady Lord Mayor Amber Lynn Thoden of Ravens Bluff, the group was ambushed and ensorcelled with a deadly combination of a curse and geas that left the members of the Flight unable to fight nor defend themselves. The aide to the mayor, Karran Mystamere, tasked a group of hand-picked heroes to get aid from a powerful priest, secretly an archlich. The group traveled to Mossbridges and King's Reach, eventually tracking Athoomb to the Troll Mountains. The heroes were able to secure the archlich's help via payment of magic items or a debt of servitude. Subsequently, the adventurers faced another ambush by the Zhentish Red Shadows, who sought to assassinate Athoomb before he could lift the geas.

## The Voice of a Lyre

The Voice of a Lyre is a one round adventure module set in the Living City organized play program. It was published in July 1995 and is intended for adventurers of any level.

Synopsis
By happenstance, a group of adventurers of the Living City came across a young performer, Eric Luffson, at the Sleepy Dwarf Tavern. The young man performed The Ends of the Brotherhood of Mann, a song he wrote about his father's curse – the result of a misadventure and betrayal decades prior. The adventurers agreed to find all past members of the Brotherhood of Mann to assemble the Seal of Mystra and confront the betrayal who had been trapped within a Shrine of Mystra. Subsequently, the adventurers tracked down Knile, Leland, Mehail, Quillion, and Seejil, slaying the betrayer and returning bard Luff's lyre and lifting the curse.

## The Curse of Red Death

The Curse of Red Death is a one round adventure module set in the Living City organized play program. It was published in March 1992 as the eighth Living City tournament module and is intended for adventurers of any level.

Synopsis
In the early-to-mid 14 century DR, Sir Ian Glae James Graham wed Lady Holly. To celebrate the event, the happy couple exchanged wedding gifts. The bride used stone shape to shape red marble into a sword. Eventually, Sir Graham met his doom fighting a group of clerics of Talos. As he laid dying in a ravine, Tyr decided to reward the paladin by merging his soul with the Red Death bastard sword. Ten years later, a drunken Talassan priest was heard bragging of a paladin's death, and the rumor reached Holly Graham, who ran a cidery outside of Ravens Bluff's walls. She tracked a band of trustworthy adventurers and asked them to investigate the rumors and find out her long-lost husband's fate.
The adventurers followed the rumors of Talassan activity as it led them to the same ravine where Sir Graham died, where clerics established a stronghold and were planning to move against Ravens Bluff. Subsequently, the heroes defeated a group of evil priests after convincing an old hermit to return the magic sword he had hidden a decade before. With Red Death's help, the adventurers persevered and returned the sentient weapon to Holly. Once the bastard sword met Holly's hand, her lost husband reappeared in flesh and blood, looking like he had not aged in a decade.

## The Ugly Stick

The Ugly Stick is a one round adventure module set in the Living City organized play program. It was published in August 1992 as the tenth Living City tournament module and is intended for adventurers of any level. The module received a reprint in Polyhedron 89 in 1993.

Synopsis
A group of adventurers of the Living City set out to investigate customers of the famous Poston Plateau Resort mysteriously loosing their attractiveness. they discovered that a resort employee named Fawn, an unnaturally beautiful cleric, came to possess a duo of interconnected enchanted wands. The wand of ugliness, when used, made its target unattractive – an act of evil that shifted its wielder's personality towards maliciousness and evil. After being used, the wand of ugliness allowed the wielder to use the wand of beauty to beautify a target. Eventually, the adventurers reassembled special containers that neutralized both wands and their effects, and confronted Fawn.

## The Amiable Art of Necromancy

The Amiable Art of Necromancy was a book dedicated to the arcane arts of necromancy and their practical usages, penned by Cherish Hollow sometime in or before the late 15 century DR.

Contents
The book's author recorded her musings and views on the art of necromancy and her attitudes toward outer people's opinions on the subject. Even though many frowned on necromancy, Cherish Hollow claimed that it was a "social magic." She then continued making that point by walking about her zombie servant – the creature that once was Nascent Owens. Cherish stated that the zombie remembered naught of its former life and that it found pleasure in serving his mistress tea, performing foul-smelling yet relaxing backrubs, or attacking her enemies and consuming their brains. Cherish stated that the discarded body – a husk, was given direction and purpose in the most economic sense as well as in the metaphysical sense. The author concluded by stating that necromancy was is useful to those who sought to challenge the cultural notions of death and to those who were lonely.

History
Circa the, several copies of The Amiable Art of Necromancy could be found in the city of Baldur's Gate. One belonged to the Jannath family, stashed in the Jannath estate and another belonged to Lucretious, the proprietress of the planar Circus of the Last Days.

## Thundaerlyn Hall

Thundaerlyn Hall was a meeting hall and rental market in Marsember in Cormyr during the late 14 century DR. It was the site of an attempt on the lives of the Obarskyr royal family in the .

History
After spring began in the, Princess Regent Alusair Obarskyr and the widowed queen Filfaeril Obarskyr were invited to Thundaerlyn Hall at first candlelight one evening. They assumed it was a trap, but decided to attend and spring it anyway.

There, a number of nobles, bolstered by Red Wizards of Thay led by Harnrim Starangh, attempted to end the Obarskyr line. They were somewhat derailed by a number of dragons using their breath weapons through the skylight, which led the Thayvians to counterattack with notably poor aim, shattering much of the building into ruins, and then attacking each other in the chaos. Even after that setback, the assassins were further slowed down by the intervention of Noumea Cardellith.

Structure
After the assassination attempt was fumbled by the sudden appearance of dragons, there wasn't much left. Before that point, the building had a grand roof, with spires and skylights.

On the inside, the hall had at least one grand balcony overlooking a room that ran east to west. There were many doors around the hall.

Interior
At the time of the assassination attempt, at first candlelight, the inside was dimly lit. The skylight was also rusted to the point of uselessness.

Services
The place was a rental market and meeting hall.

## The Dukes of Baldur's Gate

The Dukes of Baldur's Gate was a book dedicated to the Dukes of the city of Baldur's Gate, written in 1492 DR and reporting on the latest political situation at the time of book's release.

Content
The book coveys information on the groups that lead the Gate: the Parliament of Peers, which consisted of the city's patriars, and the Council of Four, on which the most powerful Dukes sat, including the city's Grand Duke. The book stated that this traditional structure held strong through the Gate's history, apart from occasional times of crisis.

The current state of the government in Baldur's Gate at the time of the book's publishing was, indeed, in crisis that brought changes to the administration. In the, the Council of Four consisted of Duke Belynne Stelmane, Duke Dillard Portyr, and Duke Thalamra Vanthampur, led by Grand Duke Ulder Ravengard. The changes came with the death of Duke Vanthampur and the disappearance of Grand Duke Ravengard during the events that came to be known as the Fall of Elturel. The Council remained incomplete until the Grand Duke could be returned or confirmed dead. In this time of political uncertainty, a new face appeared on the scene – Lord Enver Gortash. The young Lord came into the spotlight with grand promises of strong leadership and a strong hand to squash the rampant crime.

When Ulder Ravengard inevitably emerged alive from the Fall of Elturel, Lord Gortash received his endorsement, and the title of the new Grand Duke was sure to follow.

History
Soon after the book's printing in the, its copies found its way into the hands of inhabitants of Baldur's Gate, including The Bibliophile, a book shop run by Nansi Gretta, and the Baldur's Mouth in the Lower City.

History
In the, The Anatomy of Hag was studied by Mayrina after forming the Anti-Hag Support Group, in search of ways to stop hags' sinister and malicious plots. The book's lore eventually helped Mayrina discover the recipe for hag's bane – a concoction that could save the life of a child consumed by a hag. The crucial revelation was found in the book's 18 chapter. Some of the regain combinations tested by Mayrina during the research included failed mixtures of dragon egg mushroom with autumn crocus, and crawler mucus with fibber's trumpet and melloweed. The combination of elmorin wings and whisperlight venom showed potential but was too unstable to be reliable.

## The Unforeseen Alliance, Volume I

The untitled book that had several tentative names, The Unforeseen Alliance, Volume I, Druids and Harpers, A Fight for Good!, and The Shadowed Evil: Who Dares to Stand Against It?, was the first volume of four, all unpublished drafts penned by Roan Featherway in or before the late 15 century DR.

Contents
Volume one was nothing more than a draft, neatly scribbled in a journal. Roan Featherway's name was written inside. The book contained numerous chapters that filled the entire journal. Its inner cover had a list of publishers in the city of Baldur's Gate. The journal's cover had there titles for the book – all crossed out.

The story began as the protagonist – a mighty and brave druid named Roa, arrived at the Emerald Grove, summoned there by the Emerald Enclave. Roa was alarmed by such summoning, rightfully so. The book then briefly delved into a tangent about the structure of the Emerald Enclave – an organization of fellow druids and rangers scattered across Faerûn, fighting for the natural order of things and balance of nature, civilization, and the elements. Roa was said to be the fiercest of the Emerald Enclave's fighters and defenders of the balance. The actor then went on to describe Roa as a tall and mountainous man, built like a bear or an ox. Arriving at the Grove, Roa was greeted by the place buzzing with activities, eventually leading him to meet a beautiful ebony-haired woman with eyes blue like a bluebird. Roa's good spirits quickly turned once he noticed the woman's Harper pin.

History
Roan Featherway was himself a druid of Silvanus and his work was heavily inspired by the events of the war between General Ketheric Thorm and the joint forces of Harpers and the Emerald Enclave that took place in the late 14 century DR. The draft novel's characters included the real druid of the Emerald Grove – Halsin. As of the, it remained unknown whether "The Unforeseen Alliance" ever was published, just like the rest of the drafts in the series.

## The Cost of Sorrow

The untitled book that had the tentative name The Cost of Sorrow was a romance novel and the third volume of four, all unpublished drafts penned by the amateur novelist Roan Featherway in or before the late 15 century DR.

Description
This volume was penned in a beautifully bound journal. That was once the case as the completed work was rugged with its pages ripped, replaced, and glued over, affixed to the book's spine with twine. The cover boldly read "Volume III" and hd its tentative title written underneath, followed by a number of question marks.

Contents
The third volume of Roan Featherway's work focused on the drama between Roa and the series' antagonist, General Ketheric Thorm. It included a confrontation between the two in which Roa screwed at his opponents in animalistic rage, demanding to know the General's reasons for following the dark goddess Shar and destroying the village of Moonhaven. Ketheric responded, stepping over dead Harpers on the ground, with a cruel statement that Shar knew all and he was on her holy mission. Roa claimed that the people of Moonhaven trusted the general, and his Dark Justiciar attack was a betrayal, and the General responded by saying that Shar's servants needed target practice. The story continued with a duel between the lone Silvanite druid and the Sharran General.

History
Roan Featherway was himself a druid of Silvanus, and his work was heavily inspired by the events of the war between General Ketheric Thorm and the joint forces of Harpers and the Emerald Enclave that took place in the late 14 century DR. The draft novel's characters included the real druid of the Emerald Grove, Halsin. As of the, it remained unknown whether the manuscript was ever published, just like the rest of the drafts in the series.

## The Bhaalspawn Saga

The Bhaalspawn Saga was a two-volume chapbook that told a fictionalized version of the Bhaalspawn crisis of 1368 DR. It was published in or before the late 15 century DR.

Contents
The Bhaalspawn Saga was a popular series of two novels printed as thin and poor-quality chapbooks. It presented a liberally embellished version of the historic events, flush with exaggerations, fabrications, and egregious flights of fancy. The novels followed the future Grand Duke Abdel Adrian, beginning with his departure from the fortress of Candlekeep, meeting the future High Harper of Baldur's Gate Jaheira and other enemies and allies, and ending the sinister plot of the infamous persona Sarevok Anchev. The second volume continued the story following Adbel and his allies into the nation of Amn and the city of Athkatla.

History
In the late 15 century DR, Jaheira, a friend and adventuring companion of Abdel's, owned copies of both volumes. The first book was filled with annotations from the High Harper and her amused, sometimes outraged comments. The second book suffered much more at Jaheira's hands. The volume's early chapters were defaced, and some were completely ripped out from the book.

## The Golden Lodge

The Golden Lodge was a small shrine dedicated to the Merchant's Friend, the goddess Waukeen, located in Lonelywood, one of the Ten Towns of Icewind Dale.

Location
The Golden Lodge stood close to the center of the settlement, just east of a well and south of the Weeping Willow Inn.

Structure
The shrine was a simple wooden structure that consisted of two square sections connected by an elongated hallway. Like many other buildings in Lonelywood, The Golden Lodge was built on stilts, elevated over the frozen soil with a single stair leading toward its entrance.

Interior

The temple opened up into a small square chamber, lavishly decorated by Lonelywood's standards. The entrance was followed by a carpeted walkway across a tiny pool with statues of Waukeen on each side, depicting the goddess as a beautiful young woman with an outstretched arm. A decorative railing encircled the pool, and the chamber's floors and walls were tiled. The shrine's altar stood in the northern corner of the room. To its right was a long passageway with a red and black rug along its length that led to the priest's quarters hidden behind a curtain.

The cleric's quarters was a square room of the same size as the shrine with wooded floors and a single rug near the fireplace. Its walls held bookshelves stuffed to the brim with books on the topic of trade and commerce, and the room's furnishing consisted of a desk, comfy chair, and a large bed.

Services
The shrine offered the usual array of clerical services: healing, priestly spells and rituals, as well as some mercantile activities. The temple dealt with potions and some enchanted items available in exchange for a generous donation. Tymoran magic oil of second chances was one of the temple's most notable consumables. Magic items available there included Waukeen's Defender shield, the kinetic spear created by Giddeon the Believer, an Ilmatari Three White Doves mace, the Flail of Mae, ancient Amaunator's Legacy, the nihilistic weapon called the Inconsequence, exotic Sarutobi's Stone Breakers from Shou Lung, and Mulhorandi scarab of goodwill.

In addition to the priestly and mercantile activities, The Golden Lodge performed tasks common for the clergy of Waukeen – it maintained relations with the crafters and artisans of Lonelywood, monitored trade, and aided upstart businesses and exporters.

History
The temple was established by Grand Syndar Quinn Silverfinger of Goldspires in Athkatla sometime before the . Another notable member of the clergy who served under Quinn was Nolan the Healer who served the church at The Golden Lodge until he was shipped to Targos as a "penance" for greed running too thickly in Nolan's blood. He was tasked with establishing new trade with Lonelywood and traveled to other settlements in the area, trying to convert drunks and barbarians into the Waukenaar faith. In the, Nolan of The Golden Lodge joined the Targos Guard as a healer to aid the town against the attacks of the Legion of the Chimera that plagued the region.

Aged Quinn Silverfinger remained in charge of the temple as late as the .

Description
By 1281 DR, Thom was an aged human man with light skin tone, his hair whitened and eyesight dulled by age.

Thom and his late wife lived in a cabin in Lonelywood, elevated from the frozen ground and perched atop tall stilts, next to the town's windmill. The cabin's entrance was only accessible via a tall ladder.

History
By the, Thom Farold was a widower. He honored his late wife by building a large boat that could transport up to seven people. Selara, the boat, was named after her. During the late 13 century DR, Thom could often be found fishing with his friend, a not-so-humble fisher named Young Ned. In his later years, Thom took on building small boats, with Selara being his biggest project, when he was not over-indulging in ale.

## Theocracy of the Deep Ones

The Theocracy of the Deep Ones was a morkoth kingdom beneath the Sea of Fallen Stars that lasted for a 109 years, existing from  to, and was one of the big powers of the Third Epoch of Serôs.

History
The Theocracy of the Deep Ones arose in the wake of the Sixth Serôs War's end in the .

A hundred and two years after their rise to power, the Theocracy instigated the Seventh Serôs War when they attacked the merfolk empire of Hmurrath and the shalarin kingdom of Es'rath on two fronts. From the former, the morkoths stole a powerful artifact known as the Emerald Eye of Kyron. The Emerald Eye would play a major role in the war going forward, as the morkoths used its powers to great effect.

In the, during one of the last battles of the War, a legion of elite morkoth warriors slew the storm giant adventurer Lorthan and took from him the legendary double-bladed sword Krakenscourge. Determined to reclaim the weapon that had long been lost to them, the hidden and normally isolationist Triton Protectorates unexpectedly joined the fray. The tritons not only reclaimed the Krakenscourge from the morkoths, but their intervention dealt a crushing blow to the Theocracy of the Deep Ones. With their war lost, the morkoths were forced by the tritons to scatter and flee to even lower depths of the Inner Sea.

The Shadow's Blade was a weapon specifically designed to be used by assassins and was in high demand among those who used blades to settle differences. The following year, one such blade belonged to Renal Bloodscalp of the Shadow Thieves of Athkatla in Amn. The sword was offered as a reward to the guild's allies who would help Renal uncover fellow thief Mae'Var's treason. Soon after, the sword fell into the hands of another Bhaalspawn—the thief Viekang in the town of Saradush.

## The Whistling Gallows

The Whistling Gallows, previously known as Skeld's Place, was a small historic tavern and an inn, located in Lonelywood, one of the Ten Towns of Icewind Dale.

Structure

The inn was a large log building with two stores located close to the heart of Lonelywood.

Interior

The inn's large taproom opened up as soon as a guest stepped through the front doors. The entire interior could be described as rustic. The log walls were abundantly decorated with a collection of antlers and taxidermied beast heads. A firepit was at the taproom's center, with roasts slowly turning, dripping fat and juices into the flames underneath. Long wooden tables and benches were spread around the room, illuminated with candles. Directly across from the main entrance stood the stairway to the second floor. To the left of the stairs stretched a long barstand made out of a single massive sawed tree trunk with tree stumps in front of it instead of bar stools. Shelves full of alcohol, kegs, and bottles were behind the bar, as well as a small metal tub to wash tankards in.

To the entrance's left side, a small hallway was locked behind a door. From there, the proprietor accessed a small kitchen and the cold storage. On the opposite side was the room used by the tavernkeep as lodgings. It was a small room with a huge mirror built into a wall. The mirror, however, was "magical," if some were to be believed. It could be opened, allowing passage to a secret room used by Kieran Nye as a wizard's lab, filled with books, enchanted trinkets, reagents, and a crystal orb perched atop a pedestal, radiating blueish glow. The lab's walls were draped in expensive-looking blue tapestries. Some of the curious items there included a rogue stone, a robe of the neutral archmagi translocation arrows, a flask of oil of speed, and a scroll of a rare mage spell – seven eyes.

The second floor was fully used to house guests – a long hallway of rooms with various levels of decoration, but most included a nightstand, a bed, a wash tub, and some had more mounted beast heads and wardrobes. The hallway was decorated with several hanging paintings.

Services
The Whistling Gallows offered warm beds, strong drinks, and food to its guests. In 1281 DR, the inn had a resident drunkard who was also the entertainment – bard Murdaugh. If one were to discover Kieran Nye's secret, the wizard offered to trade some of his most precious magical artifacts in exchange for their silence.

Some of the drinks sold at the inn were simple cheap ales, Iriaeboran North Brew, Knee Cracker Cider, Luskan stout, Winter Wine, Bitter Black Ale, Cormyran brandy, and Moonshae whiskey.

History
As of the, there were no settlements north of Termalaine. The land surrounding the Lonely Wood held nothing more than several logging camps and trapper huts. The town truly was born with the construction of the famous Whistling Gallows Inn. Back then, the inn was better known as Skeld's Place, run by a violent half-ogre named Skeld who clobbered unruly patrons and used a tree outside the inn to hang those who wronged him. At night, cold northern winds whistled between all the hanged frozen corpses. Soon after, houses started appearing around the inn, and more people started settling in the secluded northernmost town. Only shortly before the, Lonelywood was recognized by the council of the Icewind Dale. Skeld died sometime before 1281 DR, and the inn was purchased by Kieran Nye, an old Tethyrean wizard who at one point was a member of the organization that would eventually be known as the Host Tower of the Arcane. Kieran was a deserter, and the Host Tower wanted him dead, so he kept his past affiliation a secret.

By the, Kieran's great-granddaughter had taken over the inn. Kiera Nye did not like adventurers poking around the inn's backroom, nor did she like them entering her great-granddaughter's study that was still hidden behind a mirror in the back.

Appendix
Trivia
The paintings on the second floor are easter eggs depicting in-game renders from Planescape: Torment depicting a lavishly-dressed female aasimar from Sigil and one of Nameless One's companions – the feline-looking tiefling Annah. Another painting depicted the in-game art of the Sea of Moving Ice.

## The Glitter Gala

The Glitter Gala was a jewelry and gemstone shop located in the Bloomridge neighborhood of the Lower City of Baldur's Gate in the late 15 century DR.

Location
The Glitter Gala was located on Wendserpent Street, down the street south from the Facemaker's Boutique and the Manor Gate of the Old Wall, which connected the Lower and Upper Cities. It occupied the first floor of a two-story building with the Chromatic Scale music store above it.

Interior

Inside, the Glitter Gala was a collection of displays, showcases, and chests, with its walls decorated with paintings. The area behind the counter hid a cellar hatch.

Services
The Glitter Gala sold non-enchanted jewelry and gemstones imported from Amn, Cormyr, and even such faraway places as Damara.

History
In the, during the Absolute crisis, the shop was run by Mme Omotola. One of the individuals who sought employment at the time was Ellswin Glimrock, an artisan refugee from the city of Elturel. Ellswin wrote to Omotola, praising her glittering shop and offered her services as a resident jeweler.

The same year, The Glitter Gala was contracted to craft Lady Firelia Jannath's wedding rings for the ceremony that took place at the High Hall.

During the 1492 DR, one of Madame Omotola's Glitter Gala business partners or investors was Lord Enver Gortash, secretly one of the leaders of the dreaded Cult of the Absolute. Omotola's business also supplied other fanciful shops with gemstones, such as Figaro Pennygood's Facemaker's Boutique.

## Thorm

House Thorm was a once-powerful noble house in the Western Heartlands of west Faerûn. They were based at Moonrise Towers in Reithwin within the Shadow-cursed Lands.

History

In the, a great battle fought between Dark Justiciars of Shar and druids and Selûnites; hundreds were slain. Involved in the conflict was one Malus Thorm, who made a catalogue of the dead, with their names, means of death, and possessions. This was recorded in a document kept within Reithwin's House of Healing.The document "Reithwin Necrology" in Baldur's Gate III, written by Malus Thorm, dates the battle to 986 DR. Since this is centuries earlier than other events for the Thorm family, only mentions Malus, and is against Selûnites rather than Harpers, it is presumed to be a separate conflict from that led by Ketheric later.

By the 14 century DR, Ketheric Thorm had risen to become the family's patriarch. He was married to Melodia Thorm and they had a daughter, Isobel Thorm. The family were firm followers of Selûne, with Ketheric converting to the Moonmaiden with his marriage to Melodia.Only Ketheric, Melodia, and Isobel are confirmed to have followed Selûne, but presumably others did too. At some point, Ketheric commissioned Morfred to build Moonrise Towers in Selûne's honor. Moonrise Towers even served as the base of the Crescentcoat office of the High Heralds in the mid-to-late 14 century DR, with Naernythra Thaloudyn filling the office circa 1367 DR.

However, Melodia died, leaving a grief-stricken Ketheric to raise Isobel alone, and his condition worsened when Isobel died as well. Lost in his grief, Ketheric renounced the Moonmaiden and turned to Shar, the Lady of Loss. He eventually tricked his daughter's lover, Aylin, into the Shadowfell to become a conduit to fuel Ketheric's immortality.

Ketheric Thorm then led an almost-successful campaign to wipe out Selûnite sympathies or holdouts. In a winter around, the Dark Justiciars under Ketheric fought against the Harpers and the Emerald Enclave and claimed the victory. The Harpers unsuccessfully petitioned for surrender, leading Ketheric to wipe out his enemies while the druids of the Emerald Enclave retreated. Further, a secret deal was struck between Raphael and Morfred, still a Selûnite-in-secret, to wipe out Ketheric's Dark Justiciars. Yurgir and his merregons, employed by Raphael, proceeded to decimate the Dark Justiciars, including Ketheric himself. Before his death, however, Ketheric laid a shadow curse upon the land that persisted long after his death.

Over a century later, Ketheric was brought back from the dead by the god Myrkul to be his general, tasking him with forming an alliance with the other Chosen of the Dead Three and bringing death to the world, offering the resurrection of Isobel as payment. Ketheric accepted, working with the necromancer Balthazar to give Isobel new life. After returning to life, Isobel was frightened by the sight of her "changed" father, fled to the Last Light Inn, and uncovered her father's workings with Shar, Myrkul, and the shadow curse. Unwilling to let his daughter put herself in danger, Ketheric planned to retrieve her, but became preoccupied with establishing Moonrise Towers as the new base of operations for the Cult of the Absolute, as instructed by Myrkul. In the, Isobel medt with Jaheira and her Harpers, who were also seeking answers to the sudden emergence of Absolutists.

Already extinct by that time, House Thorm lost Ketheric to a group of adventurers, who had also defeated Malus, Thisobald, and Gerringothe Thorm prior to engaging Myrkul's chosen, leaving Isobel as potentially the last Thorm.

Known Members
 Ketheric Thorm, the patriarch of the family.
 Isobel Thorm, Ketheric's daughter. A cleric of Selûne.
 Melodia Thorm, Ketheric's deceased wife.
 Thisobald Thorm, a man who worked at the Reithwin brewery and possibly Ketheric's son.Thisobald's relationship to Ketheric is unclear. When speaking to him, Thisobald introduces himself as "Son of Thorm" and refers to Ketheric as "father", though neither Ketheric nor Isobel mention a son or brother, respectively. Considering that Ketheric and Balthazar resurrected Isobel, it is possible that Thisobald is another resurrected relative of Ketheric's and refers to him as "father" not in a familial sense, but as a religious leader or perhaps even "creator". "Son of Thorm" could be him referring to a different Thorm other than Ketheric, or the family as a whole.
 Malus Thorm, Ketheric's uncle and a surgeon at the House of Healing.In Tissue and Organ Register found within the House of Healing, Malus designates himself as Ketheric's uncle.
 Gerringothe Thorm, a woman who worked at the Reithwin tollhouse.
Possible Members
 Eldebuck Thorm Fendarl, self-styled High Knight-Emperor of Fendarl's GateWhile the name "Thorm" is common in Realms sources, it is most often a given name, not a family name. It is unknown if Eldebuck Thorm Fendarl carries his middle name as a given name or family name, but as equally eccentric nobility living just upriver of the Thorms, he is included here as a possible relation.

## Thirsty

Thirsty was Marlin Stormserpent's pet stirge in the late 15 century DR.

Personality
Unlike other stirges, Thirsty liked to sample blood from many different people, instead of draining one target to death. The creature was quite affectionate with its master, letting itself be petted. It was not comfortable with magic, digging its claws deep and defecating copiously when it saw any.

Abilities
Marlin Stormserpent often painted Thirsty's beak with a paralyzing poison. He had also trained the stirge well enough to know it was to go for a selected target first.

Relationships
Thirsty was of course Marlin's pet. Unknown to him, the evil archmage Manshoon sometimes took direct mental control of the stirge. It didn't like blueflame ghosts.

History
Marlin Stormserpent brought Thirsty to Castle Obarskyr in Suzail, hidden within his jerkin, when he came with a retinue to steal the Wyverntongue Chalice under cover of darkness. During the one skirmish they had with Purple Dragon knights on patrol, Thirsty was instrumental in paralyzing the one who split out from the group to summon reinforcements. After retrieving the chalice, when Marlin found that Verrin, one of his henchmen, had betrayed him and shut a gate he meant to use to escape, he sent Thirsty through the gate to paralyze him and harry Marlazander, a bodyguard of his rival nobleman Rothglar Illance, also standing behind the gate. He also used Thirsty to kill his own men once safely at home, to prevent the secret of his seizing of the Chalice getting out.

Marlin again hid Thirsty in his jerkin when meeting the city watch later, the day he was informed of Gaskur's murder, though he did not ultimately call on it.

Thirsty was later eliminated by Mirt after it tried to attack him as the man entered the Royal Palace of Suzail. Before the killing, Mirt had been last seen escaping out of Stormserpent Towers, where he had an altercation with Marlin and his co-conspirators after Marlin had realized he was not a blueflame ghost.

## Thallow

Thallow was a species of plant found growing across the Eastern and Western Heartlands, favored for use in personal hygiene.

Description
Thallow leaves were large, green, and almost rubbery, somewhat reminiscent of the rhubarb plant leaves. The leaves' toughness allowed for the use in personal clean up after nightsoil egestion, especially when on the road. Thallow leaves could also be washed to be reused later. They retained their usefulness and tough fibers for about three days when carried in a pack or a wagon. After three days, thallow shriveled and became fragile.

## The Skinburster

The Skinburster was an enchanted halberd that allowed the wielder to accumulate force energy, created sometime before the late 15 century DR.

Powers
The Skinburster's enchantments made the weapon emit a gentle yellow light in which its curved blade resembled an unnerving smile. The weapon also possessed a simple +1 enchantment that made its blade more deadly, and it guided the wielder's aim towards the target. Lastly, the weapon's skinburster force magic imbued the wielder with a charge of magical force energy upon a successful strike, making them a force conduit for twelve seconds. By itself, this enchantment had little utility but could be synergized with other magic items that allowed for the release of the accumulated force.

History
As of the, The Skinburster belonged to Inquisitor W'wargaz of Crèche Y'llek. The weapon was stored in W'wargaz's quarters in the ruined Rosymorn Monastery, in the chamber that once hid relics of the monastery.

## Thornatar

Thornatar was a War Wizard of Cormyr in the late 15 century DR.

History
In the aftermath of the massacre during the Council of the Dragon in late Mirtul of the, Thornatar reported to Glathra Barcantle on the status of the castle. Per his report, wounded nobles had been returned to their lodgings with an active listening spell on them. Of the spells, three had been abruptly broken, he believed, by hired mages, while the rest had not revealed anything of note.

Glathra Barcantle told him to continue listening, especially for Lords Emmarask and Halvaeron. Shortly after his report, the Marchioness Immerdusk, Storm Silverhand, arrived accompanied by the mask dancer Amarune Whitewave and demanded to speak to King Foril Obarskyr I, who was in seclusion after the attempt on his life.

## Thayan outpost (Evernight)

The Thayan outpost in Evernight, also known as Evernight's Thayan Enclave, was a base from which agents of Thay were able to make their presence felt within that city. The outpost also overlooked and maintained a shadow crossing from which Thayan agents could arrive in the Shadowfell from Neverwinter's Neverdeath graveyard on the Material Plane.

Location
It was located south of the river of lava that flowed through Evernight and was not far from the Haunted Pier and the Deaders Market. It was within sight of the small hill on which the portal from Neverdeath was located.

Structure
The outpost was located within a warehouse that was blackened from fire damage.

Activities
The outpost served as a headquarters for Thayan interests in Evernight, particularly in managing the portal, overseeing traffic along the Shadowfell Road (and paying the city for the privilege of using it, generally in the form of living victims for the undead citizen to consume), and keeping an eye on things in the Shadowfell. In particular, the outpost attempted to identify spies working for Netheril, such as those operating out of the dark creeper enclave. However, the undead Tribunal of Evernight forbade Thay and Netheril from open warfare, and so the Thayans had to settle for nothing more overt than assassinations and the occasional ambush. As the Thayan's largely benefitted from the status quo, they did not feel the need to test the city's patience with them.

History
This outpost was not the Thayans' primary headquarters in the Sword Coast North at the time of its operation. Thayan machinations in the area were led by Valindra Shadowmantle, who also maintained larger bases in the Neverneath and at the Dread Ring in Neverwinter Wood.

Notable Inhabitants
As of, notable Thayans at the outpost included:
 Katrice Ansar, who oversaw the outpost and served Valindra Shadowmantle. Her primary concern was rooting out suspected but unseen agents of Netheril.
 Myros, a powerful Red Wizard who schemed to undermine the shadovar in Evernight.

Thrax's cousin was Blackclaw, the terrifying and merciless leader of the Glumguts, and Thrax was one of only three Glumguts who dared to cross him.

Along with another cousin, Vynnia, and Blackclaw's son, Blackcut, Thrax made merry by playing pranks and engaging in sneaky ventures in Evernight. Their antics mostly focused on visitors to the city, but on occasion they did things that might embarrass and thus bring down the wrath of the Glumguts' employers, Netheril, if they were discovered. This in turn meant that the three youngsters ran the risk of invoking Blackclaw's wrath, although they believed they would be fine because Blackcut was his son.
