## The Painted Boat

The Painted Boat was one of the more unique eateries and event spaces, a floating structure that once was anchored  off of Ravens Bluff's harbor and jurisdiction in the waters of the Fire River, later, relocated to the shores of the Ladyrock neighborhood by the late 14 century DR.

Location

The original Painted Boat stood on pilings around  into the Fire River. The rebuilt restaurant was placed on the southwestern beach of Ladyrock on the laneway called the Ladyrun.

Structure

The Painted Boat was a small wooden building constructed out of driftwood and shipwreck materials. The restaurant stood on stilts over the waters of the Fire River, affixed to a submerged sandy shoal. It consisted of two floors and an attic in the building's peaked roof, shingled with salvaged red, brown, and dark yellow clay tiles. Both floors had windows that were usually kept open, apart from when it stormed.

The first floor stood on a  elevation over the water level, staying protected from storm waves, looming over a landing dock, which was connected to the kitchen via a dumbwaiter big enough to haul up barrels of drink and produce. The first floor had twelve stout docks for customers to tie their boats to. After arriving, they were faced with ladders that led up to the restaurant's first floor and its sizable outside dance deck that was twice as big as the entire building.

Outside, one could find a single swift mainland sloop called The Flying Fish tied to the docks. The ship belonged to the restaurant's owners in the 14 century DR and could fit three or four people and their baggage.

Interior

The upper floor and the ceiling were supported by thick ship masts, both inside and on the outer terraces. The masts and the materials used to build the establishment gave it a rustic and maritime feel on the inside and the outside. The dining room consisted of several large collapsible trestle tables that once were doors on wrecked ships. The seating was a collection of mismatched stools, and high-backed chairs cobbled together out of old barrels. The dining room walls were decorated with various pieces of naval equipment, such as anchors, capstans, pulleys, ropes, lanterns, figureheads, spyglass, scrimshaw, dried sea creatures, shells, and even whale vertebrae. The room was heated by lit brass braziers in winter months.

The restaurant's humble kitchen was a large rectangular room connected to the dining room via two doors. It housed several counters and sinks and a long fireplace on a massive stone slab with skewers, cauldrons, and pot hangers. The biggest piece of kitchen equipment was a metal box used to smoke and barbecue foods. The metal box was built into the floor and had its own chimney. Pots and pans were stored, hung from the racks attached to the kitchen's ceiling in the back, while spoons, knives, dippers, tongs, and other utensils were stored in racks along the walls. Diners' utensils were made of pewter, and plates and cups were carved out of wood. The kitchen was also well-stocked by its pirate owners with swords, butchering and carving knives, gaffs, and loaded hand crossbows.

The second floor was used as the owners' spartan living quarters that consisted of sturdy wooden beds, stools, mirrors, weapon racks, and some small tables, with sea chests used for storage. The two bedrooms were separated by a reinforced strong room that was a combination of a safe and a closet. The restaurant's attic was inaccessible to all but the owners, and they didn't care to share what was stored there.

Atmosphere
The Boat was a quaint establishment despite its clientele of typically boisterous sailors and laborers.

Services
The Painted Boat's grub was well seasoned, evident by a collection of herbs and spices always present in the kitchen: garlic, onion, dill, chervil, fennel, marjoram, sage, tarragon, and thyme. To no surprise, the restaurant's menu was dominated by the catch of the day fish, some of which was seasonal and not found on offer daily. Some of the irregular fish and seafood included dolphin, catfish, bass, tuna, mackerel, cod, lobster, crab, clams, oysters, scallops, kingfish, shrimp, crayfish, pompano, shark, flounder, grouper, frog's legs, octopus, squid, and redfish. The restaurant also had a variety of popular soups, stews, gumbos, and jambalayas on the menu. Some of the soups of the day included pea soup, mushroom soup, clam chowder, vegetable soup, chicken soup with rice or barley, and a spicy vegetable mix. Apart from these dishes, the restaurant offered barbecued pork, chicken, and curried goat. The most favorite dish, the restaurant's specialty, was a large casserole of fish, crab, oysters, and shrimp, with rice and vegetables. All orders were accompanied by a side dish, a choice between rice, oats, barley, and bread. Salads were sold as their own dishes and were flavored only with oil, vinegar, and salt. As for the desserts, the Boat offered nuts, fruit pies, and torts.

Notably, the Painted Boat provided entertainment to its guests. The music played at the eatery consisted of tambourine, recorder, cymbal, bell, and drum melodies, accompanied by bellowing of sea shanties, spicy songs, and spirited ballads. Some of the oddest acts that found their way to the restaurant included balladeers, jugglers, fire-eaters, trained animals, clowns, and tumblers. The music was accompanied by dancing couples on the dance deck. On some nights, when the darkness fell on the dance deck, it turned into an arena for dog or cock fights.

Bill of Fare
Fish
Dolphin, tuna, grouper (1 sp) • flounder, mackerel (10 sp) • kingfish, pompano, redfish (2 sp) • bass, river (15 sp) • bass, sea (12 sp) • catfish, river (5 sp) • frog's legs (3 sp) • shark cutlets (2 sp)
Shellfish
Oysters, clams (1 sp) • mussels, scallops (10 sp) • lobster (2 sp) • shrimp (1 sp) • crabs, river crayfish (5 sp) • octopus, squid (3 sp)
Specials
Catch of the day (7 sp) • soup of the day (2 sp)
Drinks
Ale, two gallon keg (2 sp) • ale, mug (1 cp) • beer, gallon keg (1 sp) • beer, mug (1 sp) • wine, house, gallon keg (1 sp) • wine, house, mug (2 cp) • wine, fine, gallon keg (2 sp) • wine, fine, mug (4 cp)
Bread, Eggs, Fruit
Wheat bread, loaf (6 cp) • rye bread, loaf (5 cp) • rice bread, loaf (3 cp) • raisins, one pound (2 sp) • figs, one pound (3 sp) • nuts, one pound (1 gp) • cheese, wedge (5 cp) • cheese, round (2 sp) • eggs, two cooked (1 cp) • vegetables, fresh (2 cp) • vegetables, cooked (2 cp)
Gumbos, Soups
Gumbo, jambalaya (1 sp) • seafood casserole (2 sp) • pea soup (2 cp) • mushroom soup (5 cp) • clam chowder (4 cp) • vegetable soup (3 cp) • chicken with rice soup (6 cp)
Landlubbers
Barbecue chicken, spicy sauce (3 cp) • barbecue pork, spicy sauce (2 sp) • curried goat (1 sp)
Deserts
Pie, fruit, slice (3 cp) • torts, fruit (5 cp)
Banquets
By special arrangement (per person 8 gp)

History
Brothers Ticaht and Nimtu opened the Boat as a way of turning a profit by doing legal work while doing it on their own terms. However, it never stopped the brothers from allowing certain unsavory activities to take place in their restaurant late at night. Industrious by nature and nurture, Ticaht and Nimtu were "wreckers"–salvagers of shipwrecks and flotsam, evident by the restaurant being built and decorated from just that. Some of the wrecks were caused by the brothers through luring unwitting vessels to their rocky doom via signal fires built exclusively along the dangerous shores of the Wild Coast at night, about the half-a-day journey to Ravens Bluff.

The restaurant was perched in the middle of the river for at least two hours, before it was run over by a rushing pirate ship. None of the owners, staff, or the cats was killed, and eventually, the restaurant was rebuilt on the beach of Ladyrock in Ravens Bluff proper.

Inhabitants
When the entertainment was not provided, or when the business was closed, the dance deck was occupied by fishers and loud seagulls, as well as a pair of large dock cats–Venus and Adonis, that belonged to the owners and were used as security. Once a year, the Boat's owners sold the cats' litter for a high coin.

## Thulkarr

Thulkarr was a war-leader of ancient Raumathar during the Great Conflagration.

History
Taking advantage of Narfell's weakness following battles two years prior, Thulkarr led an army of unstoppable stone constructs against them in the .The Great Conflagration started in, and the account on page 55 of The Grand History of the Realms suggests that Thulkarr's invasion occurred 6 years into the war. Attacking from the north, the army used portals to outflank and overwhelm their enemies and their demon servants. When the Nar were pushed back to Narjast, Thulkarr's successes drove Ayarch Rauthok to petition the Nentyarch to unleash their last resort: the Dark Fissure, which involved opening multiple portals to the Abyss in order to open a planar rift. This plan was enacted when Thulkarr's army arrived at Dun-Tharos, and the resulting rift caused the army of constructs to vanish and be imprisoned on Acheron. It was unclear what happened to Thulkarr in the wake of this crushing and disorienting defeat, but any Raumathari survivors fled the battle using magic.

## The Hound and the Hand

The Hound and the Hand was a book of the Tyrran faith printed sometime in the late 15 century DR.

Contents
The book retold the story of how the deity of law Tyr lost his hand to the primordial evil of Kezef the Chaos Hound. The story talked about how the gods stood united against Kezef, forcing him to the Barrens of Doom and Despair. They ended up offering the primordial a deal: if Kezef was able to break chains forged by Gond, using Cocytus metal, and reinforced by Mystra's magic, then the hound would be left alone by the deities. Kezef agreed, but only if Tyr held his hand in the hound's mouth. Kezef knew that he would not be able to break free but if he were to be chained, he could take Tyr's hand. Since then, the Maimed God was one-handed.

History
In the, a copy of The Hound and the Hand could be found in the library of the Stormshore Tabernacle in the Lower City of Baldur's Gate, stored near the altar and statue dedicated to Tyr.

## The Reviving Hands

The Reviving Hands was a pair of enchanted gauntlets that boosted the wearer's healing magics.

Description
These gilded gauntlets' lining had a message stitched into it: "Yes all right, all right, stop moaning and get up."

Powers
When the wearer of The Reviving Hands cast any type of healing spell, the target also received the effects of blade ward. When the wearer revived a target creature, they also were granted a death ward. The gauntlets also slightly boosted the wearer's physical strength and allowed them to cast the revivify spell once a day.

History
In the, a pair of the Reviving Hands was available for sale at the Stormshore Tabernacle of Baldur's Gate.

## The Butler's Cane Has a Knob on the End

The Butler's Cane Has a Knob on the End was a farcical comedy novel, penned sometime before the late 15 century DR.

Content
The novel's protagonist was the butler Vincent Raspington: a stiff-mannered and silly dragonborn man, who often was flummoxed over the romantic behaviors of noble ladies and their suitors. The dragonborn found himself in a comedy of errors with the nobles going "arse-over-teakettle" into lewd situations. One such erotic misadventure forced the massive dragonborn butler to pretend he was a timid gnome maid named Missy Wimplesnatch during a nobles' feast.

History
In the, a copy of The Butler's Cane Has a Knob on the End could be found in the Lady Jannath's manse in the Lower City of Baldur's Gate.

Appendix
Background
This is likely named for "A Wizard's Staff Has A Knob On The End", a fictional drinking song from the Discworld novels by Terry Pratchett.

## Thatmatt Oakhide

Thatmatt Oakhide, husband of Bruha Oakhide, was a commoner inhabitant of the Lower City of Baldur's Gate in the late 15 century DR.

Description
Thatmatt was a shield dwarf with a light skin tone, brown eyes, massive bulbous nose, long brown hair and a lush long brown beard.

History
In the, during the Absolute crisis, Thatmatt and Bruha faced the dangers of increased crime levels and looming war. Thatmatt was mugged twice in one month despite him always carrying a blade and the Flaming Fist outpost in the Basilisk Gate did not bother to act on the couple's reports. Like so many commoners of the Gate, Bruha and Thatmatt were unable to leave the city because they were too poor, and were too scared to stay.

## Thegglis Tefoco

Thegglis Tefoco was a caravan guard and one of the older children of Oliver Tefoco, the proprietor of the Beehive Goods and Wares general store in the Lower City of Baldur's Gate in the late 15 century DR.

Relationships
Thegglis was a child of Oliver and Kroyce Tefoco, and had a number of siblings. The oldest of them was Bubbles Tefoco, who lived in the Stonyeyes district of the Gate with her family and the newborn Dorimara. another older sibling was Dariel Tefoco who served the Flaming Fist. Thegglis' brother Crowell was a fellow caravan guard, and the youngest siblings Hemjax, Maggie, and others, still lived with Oliver and Kroyce as of the late 15 century DR.

History
In the, as the Cult of the Absolute threatened Baldur's Gate's safety, Thegglis and Crowell were stuck with their Seven Suns Trading Coster caravan at Boareskyr Bridge. The caravan's return to the gate was postponed due to the cult's threat and the city gates being closed. During their travels, the older caravan guards taught Thegglis to dual-wield a dagger with a sword, according to the letter home Thegglis penned for Crowell, who could not yet write.

## Thomas C. Quirkilious

Thomas C. Quirkilious, Maker of Musical Instruments, was the dragonborn proprietor of the Chromatic Scale music shop in the Lower City of Baldur's Gate in the late 15 century DR.

Description
Thomas was a tall male dragonborn with fiery eyes and crimson scale coloration. He had a curious and grand personality and wore expensive finery.

History
Thomas became the proprietor of Chromatic Scale some time before the . Thomas's daughter, Cate departed Baldur's Gate for Calimshan sometime in or prior to 1492 DR, where she encountered a curious snakeskin musical instrument called a slitherhorn. In her letter to Thomas, she promised to bring the instrument home and play it for him. Another friend, or possibly a family member, of Thomas's named Eryk sent him a letter talking about a metal called pyrohydram Eryk had encountered on his adventures that was  allegedly capable of producing quality pipes. Eryk planned to return to the Gate with a bag of the ore for Thomas to be fashioned into flutes. During the same year, Thomas was known to experiment with various materials in order to produce quality strings for his instruments. However, using peahen gizzards was a gross failure, ratgut was proven to be hard to work with, and catgut was a failure, despite being better suited for string making than sheepsgut.

## Think Easy

The Think Easy was a social club attached to the Gehirn Cibus restaurant deep in the Underdark, owned and operated by the mind flayer entrepreneur Brikhalna "Dutch" Ipprszhen.

Services
The Think Easy served as a select club for Dutch's friends, business partners, and other trusted associates. Because his social circle was made up of gangsters and crime-lords, he enforced the civility of his patrons by the threat of an elite team of drow assassins. This ensured that the Think Easy was kept a safe neutral ground, and high-stakes business deals could be conducted peacefully at his tables.

History
After earning great wealth as an independent businessman, Dutch became part-owner of the Gehirn Cibus restaurant, already a famed and popular Underdark location. Later, he opened up the attached Think Easy as a way of expanding his business.

Inhabitants
Aside from Dutch himself, prominent clients of the Think Easy included drow matriarch Felyndiira "Mad Money" Shi'narrvha, the hit man beholder Vikhrumn "100 Gold" Coll, the deep gnome fence Gnormahlenvaey "Squeaky" Catoneriehn, and the assassin Gray'shivnarien "the Fiddler" Taliain. The Fidder was fond of taking the stage at the club and taking requests from the audience—a disquieting experience given that was also how she opened her assassinations.

Naturally, law-enforcement types like Sir Elliot of Kness were not welcome at Dutch's establishment.

## The Golden Flute Tavern

The Golden Flute Tavern was a tavern opened by bard Dinsul in the Mortonbrace neighborhood of Ravens Bluff in the late 14 century DR.

Description
The tavern's ground floor included a bar and a kitchen. The second floor offered private booths to the customers, some VIP areas, and areas dedicated to bards' studies. Lastly, the second flood was where the tavern's guest rooms were located, often occupied by the owner's friends and guild mates.

Location
The Flute was located in the Uptown District of Ravens Bluff, a prime location near the temple dedicated to Sune, the Palace of Passion, and the Temple of Lliira.

Services
Apart from serving drinks and entertainment, The Golden Flute was used as a hall of training for beginner bards, offering them lodgings, education, and the stage. The tavern's attic was redesigned to serve as Dinsul students' housing. The only payment for the schooling was the students donating one percent of their performances' income to The Flute. Additionally, the tavern offered aid to any members of the Bards' Guild.

Each evening's entertainment acts there traditionally closed by a group performance of all the school's members and Dinsul himself, playing the Golden Dragon Flute. Each Friday, The Flute hosted a dance night or a ball with admission priced at a single golden raven plus whatever drinks the attendees purchased.

History
Dinsul's establishment of the Flute was a great achievement and a long-running project. The tavern's opening was officially announced on the pages of the Ravens Bluff Trumpeter, penned by Silvia Sinderan, who praised Dinsul as a self-made bard and an inspiration.

Appendix
Notes
The Golden Flute Tavern was run by Dinsul, a player character in the Living City RPGA games played by Frank Portala.

## The Caskhouse

The Caskhouse was the guildhall of the Brewers and Cheesemakers Guild in the city of Suzail, the capital of Cormyr.

Location
The Caskhouse was located above the the High Tankard tavern that the guild owned, known as the Witch-Duke's Bride in the late 15 century DR. The guildhall occupied a single floor, the second floor of that building that faced the Promenade.

Services
The Caskhouse was known to host long celebrations and revels filled with drinking that stretched into day-long events, open to the guild members and their guests. Some of the revels stretched into several days-long occasions that involved highcoin girls, exotic sweet treats, and retching buckets. The guildhall served only ales and massive platters of cheeses. Under Old Buck's management, the Caskhouse gained the love of the Suzail's citizens for regular and spontaneous "processions" of the guild's servers, who gave out free samples of brews and exotic cheeses fermented and imported by the guild. In the winter months, the Caskhouse had an arrangement with the city guard to bring the starving poor and beggars from the freezing streets to the guild house where they were given "warm-up" meals of cheese and beer, then given free cloaks and sacks of of cheese-ends to take with them as they left.

History
In the late 14 century DR, the Caskhouse and the guild were under the control of Oldvruk "Old Buck" Faerahowe, a jovial and sharp-tongued mountainous human man.

## Thessamel Arunder

Thessamel Arunder, the Lord of Spells, was a wizard in the mid–8 century DR.

Personality
The man was cold and haughty, fearing little more than other mages.

Relationships
He was somewhat afraid of Nasmaerae Felmorel. He took an apprentice, Faeya, at some point in or before ; she was also at least occasionally his playpretty lover. He also had a steward, who announced him. The warrior and explorer Barundryn Harbright later became his landlord. He claimed his tower was guarded by guardian ghosts of some sort.

Description
He was hawk-nosed and had sharp features. He favored high-collared robes of unadorned black.

Possessions
He wore some rings that could be made to flicker. While by 761 he claimed to own no kingdoms, he had gained noticeable lands and a tower by 767 DR, which he sold in that year.

History
Thessamel Arunder had been a guest at one of the banquets of Esbre Felmorel in the spring of the, together with Barundryn Harbright and a wandering stranger, Wanlorn. Before the dinner, Lord Esbre introduced him as being versed in matters magical and widely traveled. Beyond throwing a few barbs at Wanlorn, he also mentioned owning no kingdoms during the dinner, and choked up at the mention of the Lady of Shadows, whose name he did not know to be Dasumia; he refused to add anything about her. Later, when Wanlorn left in the dead of the night, Thessamel followed him.

About a tenday prior to the chaos of the Art in, Thessamel Arunder refused violently an offer for lands and a tower he'd acquired, the South Spire, and turned the merchants who made that offer into pigs for emphasis; at least one of the merchants was Hulder Phelbellow. A month later, while in the midst of bedroom antics, he signed a contract on his apprentice's belly, which made the same offer. She explained she'd tricked him in that way because of the duress placed by the chaos of the Art, as two men had come to kill him in order to settle scores in the last tenday alone. Thessamel then learned Barundryn Harbright was his new landlord and the backer for their offer.

## Tholone

Tholone was a baron of Galadorna during the mid–8 century DR.

Personality
He wanted to be a mage.

Description
The man was heavily scarred.

Relationships
Though he was considered a baron of King Baerimgrim, he styled himself Lord rather than baron, and openly flouted many royal decrees. He had under his service many magelings, many of them outlanders, and quickblades. He was no friend of fellow baron Maethor.

History
During his last decade, starting around, Lord Tholone had willfully disregarded the royal decrees of King Baerimgrim. In the, King Baerimgrim rode to Tholone's lands with a retinue of armed knights ready to demand his renewed oath of loyalty and back taxes. The king was attacked along the way by the green dragon Arlavaunta, leading to the wounds that left him bedridden for the last year of his life.

During the royal moot called by King Baerimgrim in the subsequent, where he'd name his successor, Lord Tholone spoke ill of Baron Hothal's offer to make peace with the Lords of Laothkund, and claimed to be the baron best suited to kingship because of the company of magelings he had assembled, which was a guarantee his reign would not be as bloodthirsty as the other barons' would be instead. His bid, to everyone's surprise, was supported by his fellow Baron Maethor, on the condition that Baron Belundrar be made seneschal of the Realm. Fellow baron Feldrin also made a deal with the king, pledging his support for Tholone's bid, conditional on the execution of Hothal, and the future elimination of Maethor. All so arranged, Tholone almost became king, but was slain by Court Mage Ilgrist, in truth the archmage Nadrathen, a Chosen of Mystra.

Nadrathen then had Tholone's body animate and speak in support of the mage's bid for the throne, which was inconsequential.

Rumors
It was said that Arlavaunta attacked King Baerimgrim on Tholone's orders. He was also said to be the worst choice for King of Galadorna and even the greatest threat to freedom and life for all Galadornans.

## The Wet Crossing

The Wet Crossing was a tavern in the settlement of Bargewright Inn in the Savage Frontier in the mid-to-late 14 century DR. It was the only tavern in the settlement at the time.

Location
It stood north of Bargewright Inn, between a rental paddock and the stables.

Structure
The building's façade displayed an ugly leaping-fish figurehead and prow, which came from the original owner's old boat.

Interior
Atmosphere
The Wet Crossing was a place of loud and lively song and dance, which the original owner had been famous for. There was much shouting and stomping and friendships being forged. However, as it was often deafeningly loud, seriously conversation and trade had to be conducted outside. Nevertheless, a good deal of business in the North was done in this friendly, noisy atmosphere.

Services
The drinks were cheap at 1 cp for a tankard of beer and 2 cp for a tallglass of wine, with quality to match: Volo described the dry white wine as "rough but good" and the red as "reeking" and "truly horrible".

History
Once, a ferryman plied the Ironford crossing over the River Dessarin in a leaky old boat, but after the building of the new Ironford bridge, he had no longer had any trade. So he dragged his old boat onto the shore and established the Wet Crossing tavern instead.

He died shortly thereafter, but his friends continued to manage the tavern on behalf of his widow, as they did through the mid-1360s DR.

## Thunderstorm crescent

The thunderstorm crescent was a magical sickle found in Eveningstar during the mid-1480s DR.

Description
The oddly shaped handle connected to a wicked metal blade that crackled with electricity.

Powers
The crescent possessed a powerful offensive enchantment that guided the weapon to its target and increased its damage. It also allowed the weapon to damage creatures unaffected by mundane weapons and it shocked targets struck by the blade. Additionally, the thunderstorm crescent improved the power of the wielder's lightning-related spells.

History
The sickle was recovered from the Eveningstar War Hospital following an outbreak of red musk zombies caused by the ranger Peron Uthe, who had been infected by the maddened druid Halsaime of Thorngap.

## Thread of Life

Thread of Life were enchanted kama from Kara-Tur, used by the healer devotees of Aido Glade.

Powers
Each of these kama bore a simple +1 enchantment that guided the weapon towards the target and slightly increased its damage, as well as made it possible to harm creatures typically unaffected by mundane weapons. However, the true power of Thread of Life was not in their offensive capabilities but in healing. Firstly, the wielder received the boon of slow regeneration as long as they held the weapon. The kama also possessed fifty charges, granting the wielder the ability to cast cure critical wounds by expending five charges, cure moderate wounds – two charges, cure serious wounds – four charges, and the cure minor wounds spell at will.

History
Thread of Life kama were created by the devotees of Aido Glade, who were present at many battlefields yet stayed impartial and did not spill blood. They harnessed the kama's magics to heal and ease the suffering of the wounded. By the late 14 century DR, some of these enchanted kama or copies made from the originals were found in the city of Neverwinter and nearby lands.

## Thult Oldstone

Thult Oldstone, more commonly known for his alias Arden Glimrock, was a mighty dwarvish berserker mercenary and war leader and crusader against the drow in the 13 and 14 centuries DR.

Description
Thult Oldstone was a tough warrior, highly skilled in the art of war, and healed swiftly.

History
Thult, who operated under a pseudonym, made a name for himself leading outcast mercenary band called The Oldstones, against the drow in the 1200s and 1300s DR across the Underdark tunnels in Sembia, Dragon Reach, and the Vast. The band consisted of a number of dwarves exiled from various clans across Faerûn, who clawed back into the dwarvish society's good graces, defending the Stout Folk from drow attacks. Thult Oldstone's squad fought the drow with savage determination, using self-made explosives to bury their opponents alive. Thult's career as a war leader was long and fruitful until his disappearance in the . Following the disappearance and his uncertain fate, The Oldstones' numbers suffered losses, and gradually, fewer and fewer recruits sought to join. The band continued strained activities but was believed to be either dead or disbanded by the end of the .

## The Unburdening

The Unburdening was a textbook used to teach Sharran initiates the rituals of Unburdening and the Mapping of the Heart, printed sometime in or before the 15 century DR.

Content
The ritual of Unburdening began with the agents of the Church of Shar identifying a person of interest amongst the people who sought the aid of the House of Grief in Baldur's Gate. Once the target paid the tithe to the temple, they were guided to partake in the Mapping of the Heart, a ritual performed by a ranking member of the clergy known as the Inquirer of Grief, who questioned the target verbally whilst performing a thorough mind-ream, searching every corner of their memory for anything that would be of use to Shar. Once the mind-ream and questioning were over, the target was guided into the depths of the Cloister of Sombre Embrace to face the Mirror of Loss. While facing the mirror, the target was guided through the process with prompts from the Inquirer of Grief, giving up part of their memories to the artifact. The Mirror of Loss took the memories that the target sought to forget, which were memories of value to the church, and all knowledge of the rituals and the hidden Sharran cloister.

History
The Unburdening was used by the acolytes of the Cloister of Sombre Embrace, hidden underneath the House of Grief in the Lower City of Baldur's Gate in the late 15 century DR.

## The Healing House

The Healing House was a home and place of healing in the settlement of Bargewright Inn in the Savage Frontier in the mid-to-late 14 century DR. It was owned and managed by Chanczlatha Luruin and his family.The unnamed "pharmacist who specializes in sick pack animals" in The Savage Frontier p. 28 is presumed to be Chanczlatha Luruin.

Location
It stood in the lower part of Bargewright Inn, in the northeast amongst the paddocks.

Services
As well as serving as the Luruin family home for Chanczlatha, his wife Baerlatha, and their many adopted children, the Healing House was also his office and place of work. A cleric of Lathander, he was both physic and animal healer, treating people and beasts alike with herbs and healthy broths more than his magic, and fairly successfully. His patients regularly included folk who'd run into perils on the way to Bargewright Inn and were taken to his house, and he would never leave the settlement. He also had a specialty in pack animals, given the livestock, travelers, and traders that passed through.

Chanczlatha usually charged 5 gp for a visit and 6 gp to provide care over a full day and night. He also charged for his divine spellcasting, but the followers of Lathander were treated free of charge. The profits went back into purchasing medicines and animal feed; the Luruins were usually lacking for coin.

One of the nearby paddocks belonged to the Luruins and here they cared for large unwell beasts. Here, travelers could sell aged, weary, or unwell mounts to the Luruins for 5 sp, or if needed purchase a recovering mount for 8 sp; the price was negotiated for especially small or poorly specimens. They would care for and keep alive sick and injured animals that others might abandon or euthanize.

Chanczlatha was aided by his family in his efforts. Baerlatha was a capable wizard who brewed potions and tended animals in the paddock, as well as raised the family. She would also cast spells for hire if requested, asking 1,000 gp for lesser spells and 2,000 gp for greater spells. She would never go beyond sight of Bargewright Inn's walls, however.

## Threesteel

Threesteel was a spell that turned a blade into three seeking missiles.

Effects
The instant a blade was selected by its carrier for use in threesteel, it shimmered briefly and split into three blades. Each flew forth on its own, striking at targets the spell-user intended within close range. For the duration of the attack, the weapon was magical, if it wasn't already. Whether it was or not, the weapon would not survive the spell. Earlier reports of the spell instead reported that the blade could be within  of the caster, and had similar range, as well as the ability to do harm to any creature bar those affected only by the strongest magical weapons.

Only blades that a man-sized wielder could reasonably use (so, as large as a greatsword at the most) could be affected. Per earlier reports the spell required only the metal be three-quarters or more present, and required only a blade, not necessarily a weapon.

Components
The spell had only a verbal component.

History
The spell was first developed by Delgarth of Sumbarim.

The mage Ilbryn Starym knew an equivalent spell as far back as .

The drow-dragon Nurvureem knew this spell.

## The Dead Place

The Dead Place was a stretch of forest near Starmantle that was briefly cleared of most wildlife in the  by the actions of Saeraede Lyonora.

Geography
The area contained a ruined town that had since become mounds and thickets, with especially large shadowtop trees.

Flora & Fauna
Saliently, the area was briefly cleared of any wildlife larger than mice in 767 DR.

Government
The area was at the time within the formal territory of the High Duchy of Langalos, which was centered in Starmantle.

History
The area had a name to humans, but it had been forgotten by the 8 century DR. After winter in the, all wildlife, livestock, and people passing through the area were slain and mysteriously disappeared, leading Duke Horostos of Langalos to send adventurers such as the Frostfire Banner to investigate. The Frostfire Banner was in turn eliminated by a strange phantom mist that had taken residence in a ruined keep within the wilderness, Karsus' Keep; this mist was the undead sorceress Saeraede Lyonora. The area slowly expanded to engulf a local town, Ayken's Stump, prompting action from the Harpers, who vowed to the Duke they'd report on the location, once the Duke could no longer find adventurers or mercenaries to investigate through his agents in Reth and Westgate.

After Elminster Aumar left Ripplestones that year during his long quest to cache away enchanted items as a Chosen of Mystra, he took the road to Starmantle, going straight through the Dead Place, despite warnings from locals. Ilbryn Starym, an elven wizard who was pursuing him, was also led towards that place in Ripplestones, as was the trio of Tabarast, Beldrune, and a disguised Azuth, who were also following Elminster. An ambushing force of Sharran priests, in turn, also followed Elminster to that place, after learning of his location through scrying and agents, forcing local woodsman Uldus Blackram to guide them. Elminster, in turn, came into conflict with another party of adventurers investigating the zone, only to be lured to the Keep by Saeraede Lyonora.

Along the way, Ilbryn Starym came into conflict with a party of adventurers and killed them all, and then with the Sharran priests, whom he fled from after learning about the ruins; the released sorceries also drew the attention of the elven mage Starsunder and his momentary guest, Umbregard of Galadorna, who teleported from Tangletrees to investigate. Their teleportation activated an alarm that the archmage Tenthar Taerhamoos had set up, bringing him to the area as well.

Notable Locations
 Karsus' Keep
 Ayken's Stump

There was a small shrine to Shar near the area, though not within the Dead Place itself.

Notable Inhabitants
 Saeraede Lyonora

## The Gift

The Gift was the name given to a number of concepts related to a person's innate natural aptitude for the Art of magic, and their ability to connect to and draw on the Weave.

Inception
The term came from the belief it was granted by the gods of Toril. Indeed, deities such as Mystra could give the gift to a mortal, which Ao discouraged; Ao could also do such a thing by himself. While most priests preached the Gift came from the gods, divine action seldom bestowed the Gift permanently.

It was possible to breed a population for higher likelihood of the Gift, and people with mages in their ascendance were more likely to display it, but even Mystra and Azuth working in concert did not have the power to make it a sure thing. Sorcerers, in particular, were often considered to have draconic ancestors. Other processes were considered liable to add to the possibilities of an individual being born Gifted; those included inserting dweomer-bearing objects into the mother's body beforehand, or the parents wearing enchanted underwear prior to conception, or having spells cast on the gestating mother frequently. None of them was assured of working. Children of spellscarred were statistically more likely to possess the Gift.

Notably, the Gift wasn't equal for everyone, and some magicians bore greater innate power and affinity than others.

Awakening
Of those who had the Gift, only around a third displayed it from birth, while the majority would see it awaken at some point in their lives. Those who were affected by spells, or handled magical items, were more likely to awaken their Gift. Practicing magic constantly also made that one more likely, though it had only been the path for a rare few.

It was believed the Gift could not be stolen; however, magical ability was in fact known to have been gained only at another's expense on a number of occasions. On the occasions when people realized powers they did not have before, such events were widely understood as an awakening of a latent Gift rather than a newly created Gift. Only more extreme methods, such as replacing much of one's blood with that of a creature to which the Gift was inherent, such as a dragon, were regarded as instilling a Gift where one wasn't present.

A latent gift sometimes manifested, for those sufficiently studied and practiced in the Weave, in a dim ability to feel the ebb and flow of magic when in dreams. The Gift was also necessary for attuning to certain spell-unleashing devices, or perhaps to all enchanted miscellanea.

Testing
Temples usually tested for the Gift by casting an orison, while wizards taught a prospective Gifted the workings of a minor, safe, and simple cantrip and observing the results.

Use in Magic
In its most extreme formulation, sages spoke of the Gift as the ability to call on the Weave, and it was seen as necessary to employ any arcane magic at all, but it referred also to the ability to manipulate divine energy, and in fact some other abilities, with sufficient deftness to devise new spells and manage them appropriately. In such a view, a cleric or druid without the Gift would not be in control of their own spells available, nor would they be able to research novel magics, while a warlock would be similarly limited in spells to only those their patron actively provided. While all wizards wielded the Gift by definition, those from beyond Toril who operated methods not tuned to call on the Weave were not guaranteed that all their spells would behave exactly the same.

Those with the Gift who would go on to wield magic would most likely train to become wizards. One of the important skills of wizardry, the threefold task of visualizing the specific effects and the symbology inherent to the somatic components, which was part of casting a spell, could be learned and used to at least activate items that themselves provided a connection to the Weave, even if one did not have such a connection on their own.

Other Effects
People without the Gift wouldn't be able to comprehend the sense of magical words chosen for an incantation, while those with the Gift would intuitively understand the sense and purpose of the words in the spell, even if they were not familiar with the languages selected by the spellcraftsman. The Gift also allowed "voices in the Weave" to speak to its bearers. Some people had "innate talents" alongside their Gift or as its entirety, the ability to cast certain spells or use other effects without the need for any practice.

Frequency

The amount of people who had the Gift varied, but they were rare; in the Sword Coast during the late 15 century DR, the reported ratio of people with the Gift was about 1 in 9,000, and not even half of them would ever develop it. In contrasting, in some extensively magical races, such as elves, tritons, or tieflings, the Gift was held by a majority of their members. Later numbers, taking into account numerous magical catastrophes, put the numbers of the Gifted somewhere under six percent of the populace.

In ancient Netheril, almost every member of human society was able and expected to wield at least a few basic cantras. This carried through to the descendants of Netheril; the Shadovar of Thultanthar also had a widespread basic affinity with arcane magic, with even common soldiers having at least some ability. Halruaa, too, showed an extremely high frequency of arcanists; about one-third of them were said to cast at least one spell as of, a number that held in .

In Society
Some societies actively tested children for the Gift, including Thay. Every citizen of Thay was tested in their infancy.

The Harpers sought out those with the Gift, especially those who might be interested in joining.

Amongst ixzans, the demonrays of the Underdark, wizard ixzans had an intuitive sense for magical ability in young ixzan. On identifying one, they would defend the nascent spellcaster ferociously against others in their cruel society.

Notable or Assumed Giftless
 Archlis, a magelord, was accused of having no magic of his own by the genasi wizard Gunderal, claiming all he had were "stolen charms and looted trinkets." Whether it was true or not, the insult appeared to hit home for him.
 The Yhaunnian scion Keph Thingoleir was not able to learn or cast any arcane magic, despite all his siblings and his parents being capable of wizardry. Instead, he had a powerful affinity for the Power.
 The Cormyte nobleman Sardasper Halaunt, despite all his ambitions, was never able to master any magic to the day he died.

Giftless Magic
A few methods of magic, such as table magic, didn't require the Gift. As the Gift was a connection to the Weave, magic that did not depend on the one was expected to function without the other. However, even those lacking an intrinsic connection to the Weave were considered to bear the Gift if they could cast spells at all, by definition. Magic that was not a thing of the Weave included a few other methods beyond table magic, such as truespeech and pluma.

For those without the Gift, some powerful magic items (mostly artifacts) could provide a pathway to working magic.

## The Familiar 2/Dangerous World

Dangerous World is a short story by Andrew Foley for Baldur's Gate: Siege of Dragonspear. The story was published in The Familiar 2.

Summary
The story begins sometime during the, with the hobgoblin Grathm hunting down the goblin shaman M'khiin Grubdoubler.

During a storm, M'khiin takes refuge in a cave, where she discovers an injured drow, Baeloth Barrityl. She heals him and decides to assist him, though her efforts seem to yield little reward beyond gaining a deeper understanding of the broader world around her.

M'khiin cleverly outmaneuvers the goblins from her village who are tracking her. She arranges a clever encounter with an adventuring party called Silver Hawkes also pursuing Baeloth, forcing the two groups fight one another. M'khiin and Baeloth observe the battle and execute the remaining pursuers.

## Thundaerl

Thundaerl was an archmage and chef of Tethyr in the mid-to-late 14 century DR.

Abilities
He developed spells. His latest spell as of around  was Thundaerl's universal taster.

Possessions
He was rich.

According to Elminster, he'd been an attendee of Magefairs at some point, his visits coinciding with Mordenkainen of Oerth, and he had been the first archmage to labor as a chef in some king's court.

Some time around, Elminster Aumar came across Thundaerl in the week before meeting with Mordenkainen and learned of his latest spell. Mordenkainen mentioned the Circle of Eight had paid him a visit once whilst in magical disguise; he described the pastries the man made as "excellent". Elminster mentioned Thundaerl had grown quite rich over the last dozen years in Selgaunt and devised a spell that revealed poison, Thundaerl's universal taster.

In the, Thundaerl returned to Tethyr, trying to take the post as the palace chef, but came into conflict with the current chef, Gisbertus. Thundaerl eventually became chef of the Great Hall, where he was in charge of feasts rather than day-to-day matters.

## The Hells Unleashed

The Hells Unleashed was book dedicated to the Nine Hells, penned sometime in or beofre the late 15 century DR.

Contents
One notable chapter of the book was titled "Nine Steps to His Infernal Throne" and provided information on each of the nine layers of Hells and their rulers. It also listed spell components required to cast a scrying spell onto each of the Hells' dukes. To scry on the Archduchess Zariel of Avernus, one required a heliotrope, encasing a done splinter; Archduke Dispater of Dis needed a bit of the infernal iron ore; Archduke Mammon of Minauros – a gold coin encased in petrified peat; Phlegethos' Fierna and Belial – a bit of everburn ash balanced on a scale of stone; Archduke Levistus of Stygia – a coal-black eye encased in ice of its own tears; Malbolge's Archduchess Glasya – a coronet stained with blood of three legitimate rulers; Maladomini's Archduke Baalzebul – a fat Gorian fly, gorged on a petioner's blood; Archduke Mephistopheles of Cania – a burned book of priceless lore; and lastly, the book sthated that attempting to scry on Nessus's Lord Asmodeus resuled in the caster's immidiate and permanent disaperance.

History
In the, a copy of The Hells Unleashed belonged to the mysterious unded necromancer known as the Mystic Carrion – stashed in the creature's home in the Lower City of Baldur's Gate – the Philgrave Mansion. Another copy belonged to Franc Peartree, a one-time agent, who worked for Lord Enver Gortash and was murdered in 1492 DR.

## The Army Scythe

The Army Scythes, or simply light crossbows of speed, were a variety of enchanted light crossbows that fired and reloaded at lightning speeds.

Description
Light crossbows of speed consisted of a wooden bow attached to a sharf, called a tiller. Most commonly, they were made of ash or yewwood. When a bolt was loaded in, the weapon's crossbar began to gently radiate a blue glow.

Powers
These weapons possessed a simple enchantment that increased the punch from the bolts fired out and guided them toward the targets. Additionally, they possessed lightning speed that made the weapon much quicker to be shot and reloaded, effectively doubling the number of shots one could unleash, compared to regular crossbows.

History
A large stash of The Army Scythes was discovered by the inhabitants of a short-lived human outpost in the Frozen Forest sometime before the late 13 century DR. The weapons were found in an old ruin of unknown origin. The human settlers went on using the enchanted weapons to claim large territory for themselves, only to eventually be exterminated by a large army of hobgoblins.

In the following centuries, The Army Scythe weapon ended up in a few places, including the ruins of the Severed Hand in the, the town of Lonelywood in Icewind Dale in the . In the, one such crossbow was in stock of the Thunderhammer Smithy in the town of Beregost, and Bernard, the innkeep at the Copper Coronet in Athkatla, sold one of The Army Scythes to the inn's unsavory guests.

Notable Owners
Hobart Stubbletoes, a mysterious hin adventurer who spirited the Heroes of Icewind Dale to a lost fortress in the Anauroch in 1281 DR.

## The Last Jack

The Last Jack was an inn and a tavern located in the Shutters neighborhood of the Crow's End District of Ravens Bluff in the late 14 century DR.

Location
The Last Jack was located just past the Ravensbridge as one entered the Shutters from Shadystreets, on the crossing of the Stonekeep Concourse and Karen Court.

Interior
The Last Jack was known for its taproom and a calm and comfortable atmosphere, especially compared to nearby rowdy Salty Dog. The ground floor taproom was frequented by the City Watch, making it quite safe. The taproom was always lively but aggressive, loud and rowdy behavior resulted in the problem guests being removed from the inn. Above the taproom, the Last Jack had three floors of guest rooms for those looking rest rather than food and libations. The guest rooms were small and humble, with a single bed with a rope frame topped with a straw mattress and two wool blankets, a candle-lamp, a water-ewer with a cup, and a chamberpot.

The Last Jack's food and drink was lackluster: watery beer, poor quality sausages, stale bread smothered in peppercorn butter. The inn also sold misshapen fried saltfish of unrecognizable species. However, tomato-and-onion chutney served at the inn was a truly good dish packed with hot-throat spices, useful to cover taste of other food here.

## The Maw

The Maw was a harbor located in Skullport.

Description
The Maw was located on the eastern coast of Skull Island. It's name derived from its resemblance to the gaping mouth of a great beast and the ominous implication that those who enter were effectively being consumed. The Maw was lined with multiple wooden docks, while recessed staircases wound their way up the sheer black stone walls of the harbor. At the top of these walls, large hoists were installed, designed to efficiently lift cargo to the courtyard beyond. During the unloading process, numerous guards in splint mail kept a vigilant watch, armed with heavy crossbows and tridents to ensure security.

Defenses
To safeguard the harbor from unauthorized departures and potential marine assaults, the Iron Ring has installed steel hull augers across the entrance of the harbor. These mechanisms, controlled by massive chains connected to winches located in the towers on either side of the harbor, were designed to dig into the hulls of passing ships when activated. The augers then flooded the lower decks, effectively immobilizing the vessel and preventing its escape. Several shipwrecks resting at the bottom of Skull Pool served as a testament to the destructive capability of these devices.

## The Gauntlet

The Gauntlet was an alley located in Skullport.

Description
The Gauntlet was one of the few alleyways in Skullport with a name, and was notorious for its high concentration of cutpurses, pickpockets, and brigands. The alley's name reflected the dangers faced by those who passed through, as well as the peril faced by the criminals who operated there. Violence was a daily occurrence, with numerous assaults and murders not only targeting unsuspecting travelers but also the cutthroats themselves.

In the Gauntlet, those who preyed on others must constantly be prepared to defend themselves, as success in stealing often turned the predator into prey. After a successful theft, the original thief may find themselves pursued by their own peers, as competition for stolen goods was fierce. This alleyway embodied the lawlessness and treachery that defined much of life in Skullport.

## Thimblewine's Pawnshop

Thimblewine's Pawnshop was a pawnshop in the Lower Port of Skullport.

Structure
Thimblewine's Pawnshop was a two-story establishment of fair condition.

Services
Thimblewine's was widely known as Skullport’s most reputable, if unscrupulous, pawnshop. The pawnshop's inventory included an eclectic array of items, from weapons and armor to bags and miscellaneous gear, often pawned by local patrons or sold at a discount by merchants, particularly ship captains, who'd failed to sell them elsewhere. Stock changed frequently, with old inventory regularly shipped topside and sold through Thimblewine’s contacts outside Skullport. Occasionally, a magical item slipped through Thimblewine's assessments and ended up mingled with the mundane items on display, making the shop a curious, if unpredictable, destination for those seeking rare finds.

Inhabitants
Circa 1370 DR, the shop was owned by Thimblewine, a shrewd and diminutive rock gnome. Thimblewine had earned a reputation as an astute fence with a remarkable ability to appraise the value of items rapidly. Through relentless haggling, he rarely paid more than 10% of an item's actual worth, employing his keen intuition and quick wit to press clients into accepting low offers.

One of Thimblewine's secrets was two magical items he'd acquired long ago: a medallion of ESP and a ring of human influence. These artifacts allowed him to subtly influence and manipulate his clients, often leaving them unaware that they'd accepted far less than anticipated. Many left the shop with only a handful of silver or copper for items of considerable value, bewildered by the gnome’s persuasive charm.

After Thimblewine passed away, ownership of the pawnshop was passed to his niece Krystaleen. Unlike her predecessor, Krystaleen conducted her business with transparency, purchasing reusable goods from visitors at the standard prices. However, all merchandise was priced at five times the standard cost. As of 1492 DR, the shop had quickly earned a reputation for fair buying practices, even if her resale prices were high.

## The Ends of the Brotherhood of Mann

The Ends of the Brotherhood of Mann was a ballad dedicated to the betrayal and fall of the Brotherhood of Mann, a Ravenaar adventuring troupe, penned by Eric Luffson, son of Luff, a member of the adventuring company, in the mid–14 century DR.

Contents

History
The song retold the story of the Brotherhood of Mann, a band of adventurers that fell apart after one of the group betrayed them during an adventure, angering the goddess of magic, Mystra, and trapping the group's bard, Luff, in the deity's hidden temple, cursed for twenty-five years. Luff's son grew up and became a musician in his own right, who penned a ballad in hopes that, one day, it would attract the attention of a brave hero of Ravens Bluff, willing to risk their life and help the bard fix the wrongs of the past. Eventually, Luff got lucky, and a group of adventurers of Living City listened to the song and helped the bard in tracking down the surviving members of the Brotherhood of Mann and reassembled a holy symbol of Mystra to gain entrance to the hidden temple.

## The Last Stand of the Allies of Azuredge

The Last Stand of the Allies of Azuredge was a tragic ballad that retold the story of an adventuring quartet's demise during the Time of Troubles.

Contents
The dirge's protagonists were four heroes who died in a stand against Myrkul's Legion during the Godswar. Beryghon, the group's warrior carried the enchanted weapon called Azuredge that mysteriously disappeared during the event.

History
In the late Marpenoth of the, The Last Stand of the Allies of Azuredge was performed by Arkiem Arren in the Safehaven Inn of Waterdeep. As the bard approached the song's conclusion, a curious occurrence took place: the inn's doors swung open, and a cold wind filled the taproom. Somehow, the chill air mixed with the music, and a glowing axe appeared over Arkiem's head. The bard's eyes filled with a blue glow, and as if entranced, he produced a new stanza added to the dirge. When the ballad was over, the blue axe flew across the taproom and embedded itself in a support pillar.

## The Tradeway

The Tradeway was a road in the Lower Trade Lanes of Skullport in the late 14 century DR.

Description
The Tradeway served as the primary and most expedient route into the deeper regions of Skullport. As the widest street within Skullport, it was constantly maintained, its cobblestones replaced by a labor force comprising enslaved workers and reanimated undead. Lining this prominent avenue were numerous permanent establishments offering a variety of goods and services, catering to the diverse demands of Skullport’s denizens. In addition to these fixed businesses, merchants crowded the road with temporary stalls, carts, and even improvised displays of wares, often carrying additional items to sell directly from their person.

Competition among vendors was intense, and disputes over pricing and territory frequently escalated, sometimes resulting in skirmishes that provided onlookers with both cover and opportunity to pilfer from unattended goods.

Inevitably, the presence of commerce drew panhandlers, particularly as one approached the Lower Port. Along the Tradeway, beggars lined the route, many displaying visible signs of injury, illness, or neglect as they appealed for small change. Though some of these individuals genuinely suffered from misfortune, others are frauds, seeking to exploit the compassion of others to finance their own indulgences. Among these beggars were numerous pickpockets and petty criminals, who stalked potential victims with practiced patience, awaiting the right moment to strike from concealment. Many worked in coordinated groups, as a result the safest way to travel was in groups.

## The Dawn of Any Day

The Dawn of Any Day was an instrument shop in Berdusk in the Western Heartlands in the mid-to-late 14 century DR, which also carried other goods that had minor enchantments placed upon them. The shop had a distinctive sigil: the rays of the sun rising over a harp standing atop a lute.

Description
The Dawn of Any Day was a small, dim building with simple wooden doors leading inside, which were only decorated by the store's sigil.

The wares inside were often in used or damaged conditions and were kept safe within floating orbs of glowing air, which could only be consistently opened by the shop's proprietor, Darthleene. Customers who tried to grab the orbs themselves would find them passing through their bodies harmlessly, item and all.

Location
The store was in Berdusk, nestled between the homes of wealthy merchants and the temples to Milil, Oghma, and Helm. It fronted many different streets in the city, including Lute Street, the Minstrelride, Danathar's Street, and Amble Lane. The shop appeared to be open at all times.

Wards placed upon the shop allowed its many entrances to change, appearing as though they led into small private domiciles rather than the shop itself as protection against thieves.

Services
The shop specialized in the sale of musical instruments but also carried a number of items bearing minor enchantments. There was a persistent rumor around Berdusk that these magical items had spells imbued into them that allowed the Harpers to track the items' locations.

Aside from instruments, healing potions, and items with glow-on-command enchantments, the store's stock changed constantly. The rarer items that passed through the store were often found to be more costly, as well as to have all manner of curses, conditions, or spells upon them.

## The Waterclock

The Waterclock was a landmark in the Central Trade Lanes of Skullport in the late 14 century DR.

Description
The Waterclock provided a precise means of tracking time within the perpetual gloom of the Underdark. Suspended from a massive stalactite in the main cavern, the Waterclock was positioned between the Central and Lower Trade Lanes.

The clock not only kept track of highsun, midnight, dawn, and dusk but also displays the months, the three tendays in each month, and the various holidays celebrated in the realm.

Maintaining the Waterclock's precise functionality required constant vigilance and upkeep. The moisture-rich air and the generally unfavorable conditions in Skullport necessitated frequent oiling, adjusting, and replacing of delicate parts and balances. Additionally, the springs were prone to stretching and wear, and the reservoirs had to be refilled on a regular basis. To ensure the clock's uninterrupted operation, priests of Gond worked in rotating shifts.

Defenses
To safeguard the Waterclock, its creators incorporated numerous defensive mechanisms. Tampering with the Waterclock, whether physically or magically, had dire consequences. Intruders risked severed limbs, electrocution, or volleys of darts from hidden mechanisms. In addition, hostile spells directed at the clock had a chance of reflecting back upon the caster. The device was further protected due to its enhanced durability. It was also immune to disintegrate. Any disturbance around the Waterclock was likely to draw the attention of the Skulls of Skullport, further discouraging interference.

History
The Waterclock was designed and constructed by three Gondsmen in collaboration with the gnomes Tykkyl and Tohkkal Burrwarden. The project was headed by Master Karl Gustavis Gearwizzen, a human cleric of Gond and a seasoned engineer. The Waterclock was conceived in 1369 DR in the aftermath of Halaster's Higharvestide.

## The Poisoned Quill

The Poisoned Quill was a shop in the Central Trade Lanes of Skullport in the late 14 century DR.

Structure
The Poisoned Quill was a one-story shack in squalid condition.

Description
In 1370 DR, The Poisoned Quill specialized in creating high-quality counterfeit documents and writs, ranging from travel permits to official licenses. It's owner, "Blind" Issayk had an intricate web of contacts across the Realms, which kept him abreast of bureaucratic changes that may render his forgeries obsolete. As a result, his products were highly effective, provided they were used promptly.

Through a combination of bribes, blackmail, and other underhanded methods, Issayk has amassed wax pressings of crucial governmental seals from across Faerûn, including those of Calimport, Luskan, Waterdeep, Cormyr, and Sembia. This collection enabled him to replicate a wide variety of official documents with remarkable precision. His services, however, came at exorbitant prices: minor travel writs might cost several hundred gold pieces, while more elaborate items, such as an engraved invitation to a Calishite noble’s ball or a signed adventuring license for use in Cormyr, may cost 2,000 gold pieces or more.

By 1492 DR, the shop was owned by Tasselgryn Velldarn, an archmage who was a close friend of Halaster Blackcloak. Instead of creating forgeries for clients, she instead provided a physical means of a quick exit from Skullport via teleportation circle. She was capable of bypassing the teleportation restrictions of Undermountain due to a series of enchantments cat by Halaster.

## Thorn Hollow

Thorn Hollow was a group of shallow caves in Thorngap, a druidic circle in the King's Forest of Cormyr. It was briefly taken over by the druid Halsaime and used as a stronghold in the mid-1480s DR.

Description
The Hollow was a series of caverns, tunnels, and open spaces in the depths of the King's Forest.

Inhabitants
Halsaime made his home there, along with the druids Garick, Flinbeck, Thomren, Larres, Drien, and Carm Woodrusk. They lived alongside a number of wolves, bears, dire bears, and other animals. During his madness, the caverns became filled with red musk zombies and vine horrors, and the animals were driven into a frenzy.

History

During the Sschindylryn invasion of Eveningstar, the druid Halsaime received a powerful cursed staff from his friend Oriphaun Huntsilver. Oriphaun had taken it from a Shadovar agent he killed while protecting the Abyssal Planus Mechanus Nether Scroll, and correctly identified that it was a dangerous artifact best handled by the wise. Unfortunately, Halsaime was overcome by a furious madness and used the staff's power to twist nature and his fellow foresters into a force to conquer the world with.

The Harpers Kirinel Zay, Tarim Inavule, and Jussko Kwahn investigated the situation after the ranger Peron Uthe returned from Thorngap carrying the red musk disease. Guided by the tracker Garstrom Toom, their agents found Thorn Hollow and looked for Halsaime, instead finding corrupted druids and monsters. Several "corruption nodes" were scattered about the caverns, trapping the resident bears in their dens with red musk seeds that drove them into a maddened rage. After eliminating the corruption nodes and their druidic defenders, the adventurers found the dying Carm Woodrusk, who had resisted Halsaime's power and paid the price for it. With her last breath she revealed that Halsaime was hidden at the nearby Druid's Deep, sending the Harpers on one last mission.

## Thorngap

Thorngap was a druidic circle in the King's Forest of Cormyr. It was taken over by the druid Halsaime and used as his lair in the mid-1480s DR.

Description
Thorngap was made up of several interconnected groves, caverns, glades, and other natural features in the King's Forest. It included the dens of Thorn Hollow, where druids and beasts lived together, and the hidden sanctum of the Druid's Deep. Some caves reached down to the Underdark, while others were filled with water and served as secretive passageways.

History

Thorngap served as a home for druids and rangers in the King's Forest for centuries. During the Sschindylryn invasion of Eveningstar, the druid Halsaime was driven mad by his cursed staff and used its power to forcibly control nature and his fellow foresters, intending to build an army with which to attack the world at large.

After the ranger Peron Uthe caused an outbreak of red musk zombies in Eveningstar, the Harpers Kirinel Zay, Tarim Inavule, and Jussko Kwahn arrived to investigate. With the assistance of the tracker Garstrom Toom, their agents found Thorngap and looked for Halsaime at his home at Thorn Hollow, but only found frenzied druids and animals. After fighting through the defenders, the adventurers found the dying druid Carm Woodrusk, who had resisted Halsaime's power and been lethally wounded. With her last breath she revealed that Halsaime was hidden at the nearby Druid's Deep refuge, sending the Harpers on a final strike at him. While Jussko Kwahn scouted ahead and was temporarily petrified by Halsaime, the adventurers overcame his last defenders and slew him. The recovered Jussko then destroyed the cursed staff, ending the dire influence over Thorngap.

Inhabitants
The respected druid Halsaime made his home there, along with a number of other druids, rangers, and dryads, who lived alongside wolves, bears, dire bears, and other animals. During his period of madness, Thorngap was filled with malevolent wisps, earth elementals, red musk zombies, wood woads, and vine horrors. The animals were driven into a frenzy, and many of the resident folk were forcibly recruited to Halsaime's cause. During this time the bog hag Aghilde moved into a dank corner of the refuge and made herself at home.

## The Shod Talon

The Shod Talon was a tavern and inn in the city of Ravens Bluff that catered to elves and half-elves.

Location
This tavern stood along MacIntyre Path, in the Sixstar neighborhood of the city's Uptown District.

Structure
The Shod Talon was housed within an old stucco building with a slate roof, which had a  by  patio perched atop it. Outside the building was hung a sign depicting a roc with talons outstretched. Said talons on the sign were covered with steel.
Interior
Within the storage room of the building stood a spiral staircase that led up to the Shod Talon's rooftop patio.

Atmosphere
This establishment was a lively place of chatter, drink, and dancing for all manner of elves and half-elves. Humans and halflings that visited the tavern would find themselves tolerated, though not as comfortable as they would in other nearby establishments. However, the place was not nearly as prejudiced as the Ill Eagle Inn.

Services
The prices of goods on offer at the Shod Talon were higher than some other establishments within the area, but by far not the highest. And with the quality of the food and drink on offer, very few saw fit to complain about these prices.

Drinks
 Ale: 4 sp
 beer: 1 sp (for )
 Wine: 12 sp to 1 gp
Eveningfeast
 Meals: beef ribs: 1 gp • beef steaks: 2 gp • chicken eggs: 5 cp • mutton: 6 sp • roast chicken: 8 sp • roast turkey: 4 sp • vegetables: 5 cp • venison: 8 sp

In addition to food and drink, the Shod Talon offered lodgings in one of its ten rooms at a nightly cost of 1 to 5 gold pieces, usually offering this service to elves or anyone who couldn't or didn't wish to stay at one of the local inns for one reason or another.

History
Sometime prior to the,Gateway to Ravens Bluff (p. 7) states that Charles O'Kane has been Mayor for 14 years, which tracks with the later article "Pillars of Ravens Bluff" in Polyhedron #147. It also states he is 48 years old, which conflicts with the "Pillars" article and is assumed to be an error. Voron Orama came to the city of Ravens Bluff in search of a relative. While there he purchased their decrepit establishment, the Shod Talon, and rebuilt it. The new owner cared little for the name "Shod Talon", but refused to change it out of a fear that doing so would bring bad luck.It is not stated when exactly Voron Orama bought the Shod Talon. It is stated in Gateway to Ravens Bluff that Gaolla Luathe had been working for the past 30 years, but it's possible they could have been working there prior to Voron's purchase of the Shod Talon.

The Shod Talon was closed down for a time during the Three Women War, but reopened after its conclusion.

Inhabitants
The tavern was lived in and operated by the moon elf Voron Orama. The building was also lived in by its cook, the half-elf Gaolla Luathe, and the wild elf waitress Dumiriel.

## Thanadar

Thanadar of Dragonrock was an adventuring ranger through the early-to-late-mid-14 century DR, and a member of The Nine.

Description
He was tall, with graying hair, steel-gray eyes, and an urbane manner.

Personality
Though once merry and proud, he was much-changed since.

Abilities
Despite his age, the ranger was very strong in  despite a career that stretched before  and a human lifespan.

Of note, due to a curse, Thanadar had to change his name.

Possessions
Thanadar had a significant amount of magic on him, including a defender longsword, a ring of shooting stars, a girdle of many pouches, a seemingly endless supply of potions of healing in it, and a blink ring with the ability to use blink, dimension door, and teleport without error twice a day each.

Activities
Thanadar led a small band of caravan guards he'd trained himself, which operated in the Sword Coast North.

Relationships
Once one of The Nine alongside the bard later known Arnthiir Windrivv and Laeral Silverhand, after they were released from their curses, Thanadar continued to be in occassional contact with Laeral Silverhand.

Notably, Thanadar had taken the name of a grand-uncle of his', a man from Dragonrock, who had died some decades prior to .

Thanadar had gained the rare trust of the elves in Greycloak Hills and could pass through unmolested.

History
The bard was one of the Nine in, the year in which they acquired the Crown of Horns, a Myrkulite artifact; the crown put a curse on them that gave any hordling in Hades the ability to teleport without error to their presence, even across planes, by simply uttering their names. Laeral came to possess the Crown through most of that time; with its fell power, the artifact drove the adventurers to fight each other until Laeral was rescued by Khelben Arunsun. The mage then broke the curse on the surviving members, including him and the ranger, but that required them to abandon their old names.

By the mid-to-late 14 century DR, he spent most of his time heading a company of caravan guards throughout the Sword Coast North.

Rumors & Legends
It was said he kept a cache of enchanted devices in the Marsh of Chelimber.

This business was located in the northeastern quarter of Ordulin, just down the street from the Six Candles Inn.Heir Un-Apparent describes The Cat's Meow as being situated in the "SE quarter of the city", however, the Six Candles Inn is located in the NE quarter of Ordulin.

Location
The Wheel stood on The Drae, the moot of The High Ride that ran from east to west, and the Dausann – south to north. The Drae was thought to be the destination for the city's best revelry, food, and feast.

## The Yardarm

The Yardarm was a tavern that offered food and drink and catered mainly to the sailor folk of Velen, a coastal city on the Dragon's Head Peninsula of Tethyr in the late 14 century DR.

Location
The Yardarm stood on Sarnsar Street next door to The Black Boat shop.

Interior
The tavern's sprawling taproom was rustically decorated and always clean. Most of the time, it was filled with a cacophony of happy customers, conversations, and laughing. Brawls and gambling were exceedingly rare occurrences, which was favored by the staff and customers alike. The tavern only welcomed sailors and their lady companions, both escorts and girlfriends. Even though there was not an official ban on non-sailors, landlubber guests were met with silent stares that were likely to drive away most unwanted customers.

Services
The Yardarm was somewhat unique among the establishments that mainly catered to sailors: it offered quality food and drink, which came with fine dining practices, such as clean linens, finger bowls of lemonwater, and attentive wait staff. Each table had an assigned waiter, parked at a nearby stool, ready to fulfill any request.

The tavern offered beers, ciders, cordials, teas, as well as such staples as zzar, sherries, as well as outstanding wines, even elverquisst.

The menu offered warm, thick, and filling turkey broth, drizzled with sherry on colder days. The rest of the menu was dominated by a variety of stews and pastries of shelled and cake variety. Some of the more unique dishes included dumplings and sweet fruit-based sauces that, for an additional copper coin, were added to any items on the menu. The Yardarm dumplings were filled with various kitchen scraps, meats or fowl, filled with their own juices. Another staple were pan-fried potatoes in lemon, garlic, and oil. Lastly, the platter the menu called Tonguelash, was a cornucopia of wine-doused endives, hopped walnuts and pepper, pears, and herbed goat's cheese. All items were prepared with sophistication fit for Waterdeep's fine dining establishments.

Inhabitants
Rhaligo Terntevven was the tavernmaster in the late 14 century DR. His waitstaff was all comprised of homey lasses who treated all their clients as if they were their favorite uncles.

## The Simbul's tonguelash

The Simbul's tonguelash was a curious spell created by Alassra Shentrantra Silverhand, the Witch-Queen of Aglarond, better known as the Simbul.

Effects
When cast, the spell created a magical spectral extension of the caster's tongue. The said prehensile extension was fully controlled by the caster's will. It could perform any actions the caster could imagine with some physical limitations. The tongue could avoid danger; move akin a snake; wrap itself around something; pick up, manipulate, or throw a small object; or restrain a small object or an appendage. The Simbul herself liked to use the tonguelash to slap people's eyeballs with it, giving them a ringing headache and compromised vision due to tears. If the spectral tongue was damaged or destroyed, it disappeared without damaging the caster. The distance of the spell was the caster's eyesight.

## Thrallherd

Thrallherds were psionics users, most often psions (especially telepaths), who harnessed their mastery over the powers of the mind towards dominating the minds of beasts and other sentient creatures, forcing them to be their devout servants.

Culture
Thrallherds usually had a minor menagerie of enthralled creatures, who were referred to as either their thralls or believers. They preferred to delegate most tasks, including their own physical defense, to their thralls. Rather than directly involving themselves in combat, they would order thralls to fight on their behalf.

As this path of psionics involved subverting the free will of others, thrallherds were likely to tend towards the evil side of alignments. Even if not outright evil, a thrallherd's personality tended to be domineering, controlling, and in some cases even maniacal. They might even view themselves as superior to the non-psionically gifted.

Prerequisites
In order to become a thrallherd one had to be a fifth-degree manifester, know the psionic power mindlink, have decent knowledge of psionics, and display the power to recognize when someone was lying by spending a psionic focus.In mechanical terms, a player needed to have the "Inquisitor" feat that was featured in the Expanded Psionics Handbook in order to become a thrallherd.

Abilities
Upon undertaking the path of a thrallherd, the psionicist's mind developed subtle psychic resonance, connecting them to nearby people and drawing them towards the thrallherd to serve them. The first servants of a thrallherd would arrive within 24 hours of their greater telepathic abilities awakening. If any servants died, the thrallherd's psychic call would draw in new replacements within 24 hours. All thralls were anxious and eager to fulfill the will of their thrallherd.

All thrallherds knew the power psionic charm and were able to use it more effectively than other psionics users. As they progressed in power, a thrallherd gained psionic dominate, which they likewise had greater mastery of. A thrallherd suffered less mental strain from augmenting the power to affect the likes of aberrations, animals, dragons, elementals, fey, giants, magical beasts, monstrous humanoids, and outsiders. Beyond these innate powers, thrallherds tended towards learning psionics that allowed them to manipulate others, such as causing enemies to fight amongst themselves.

Following the Spellplague, thrallherds obtained the power to use the raise dead ritual to bring their most central thrall back to life, costing them on average 500 or 5,000 gold pieces in ritual components.

Possessions
While traditionally psionics users such as thrallherds didn't need any physical tools or weaponry to practice their discipline, following the Spellplague they began using implements to enhance their abilities. Typically these took the form of orbs and staves, through which they would channel their psionic energy into powers.

Notable Thrallherds
 Rhauron, the mysterious creator of the mind-controlling gems known as the Winking Eyes of Rhauron in the 1480s DR, was believed by some to be a thrallherd psion.
