## The Burning Truth

The Burning Truth was a larger-than-life bardic band that venerated the fire deity Kossuth through explosive performances of percussive instruments, chanting, and pyrotechnics in Ravens Bluff in the late 14 century DR.

Organization
When The Burning Truth was discovered by the Bards' Guild of Ravens Bluff, the band consisted of six members: Aranwe Nauril, the lead and bongo player; Javert Lorrell, who wielded various percussion instruments and chanted; Jennith Maelstrom, a chanter who played the kettle drum; Gnorris Kneebreaker, the man in charge of a massive bass drum, playing it from within, as well as pyrotechnics; Demonius Othello Tiburian Lethario III, the handler of a Kara-Turan war gong, wielder of flames, and the group's religious advisor; and lastly, Dirtbeard, who played koto drums.

History
The band was discovered in the, by the Bards' Guild of Ravens Bluff after the recent death of The Cobalt Flame, which led many to think that the Ravenaar theater scene was to enter a lull. An aspiring politician who'd recently lost an election, Harmony of Milil, had assembled a new band, a choir of romantic youths. Yet the famous bard was not the talk of the town. In contrast with Harmony of Milil's group was The Burning Truth, a rambunctious band of drummers accompanied by heavy pyrotechnics. The band's debut was reported on by Jacinth Moonspring in the pages of the Ravens Bluff Trumpeter. According to Jacinth, The Burning Truth was looking for another singer, or, as she put it in print, "a true singer." Jacinth also complimented the band's grand pyrotechnics and found the music to be quite enjoyable.

The new band was in a bit of a brewing storm, however, as they worshiped Kossuth, the God of Fire, and their performances openly venerated the deity without approval or authorization from the Clerical Circle of Ravens Bluff. Jacinth did note that, despite the performances of Harmony of Milil being veneration of Milil and The Burning Truth's being worship of Kossuth, for most of those who listened to both bands' music, it was just that: music.

By the next year, The Burning Truth's performances were regularly hosted by the Ravens Bluff Opera House, while the band operated out of the city's Temple of Tyr.

## Thrumbo

Thrumbo was a strange beggar – a sentient zombie, who shambled across the alleys of Baldur's Gate in the late 15 century DR.

Description
Thrumbo was wrapped in rags, his face hidden under a hood and a scarf. His sickly skin and stench of decay betrayed his undead zombie nature. Unlike other zombies, however, he was fully conscious and possessed undead fortitude and resistance to all types of physical damage.

Activities
In life, Thrumbo was an uneducated beggar and this lack of knowledge accompanied him into the undeath. Whist he was attempting to coordinate an escape from the master, Thrumbo attempted to teach himself to write in common and communicate amongst the fellow beggar zombies through letters.

History
Sometime before the, Thrumbo was created by the mysterious mummy, the Mystic Carrion. Eventually, Thrumbo and several other undead servants escaped their master. In 1492 DR, he could be found hiding away in the Vonayn's home, a tiny abandoned building overlooking a harbor in the Lower City of Baldur's Gate. The undead creature seemed to have had taken to begging.

Mystic Carrion, however, would not let his creations be and was attempting to find Thrumbo and other sentient zombies through magic or via adventurers. If the adventurers were to confront Thrumbo, he would act terrified of being forced to return to the Mystic Carrion's service, revealing that he and his fellow sentient zombies were once beggars in the Gate who were murdered and raised to be the mummy's slaves. Thrumbo knew of the Mystic Carrion's true nature and could point the adventurers towards where the mummy lord kept his heart in a canopic jar – the key to its destruction. Even though Thrumbo believed that the canopic jars were hidden underneath the Carrion's manse, the mummy lord hid its heart within Thrumbo.

It was unknown if Thrumbo and other undead beggars were slain or returned to the Mystic Carrion's service or if the adventurers elected to help the poor souls, recovering the heart and destroying Mystic Carrion. Another possible outcome was the adventurers attempting to kill the mummy, neglecting to find the heart. This would result in the Mystic Carrion returning shortly after being killed and exacting vengeance on the beggars.

## The Planes mantle

The Planes mantle was a psionic mantle that granted ardents and divine minds an array of psionics powers and abilities derived from the fundamental concept of the planes of existence.

Deities

Abilities
Those who followed The Planes mantle could expend a psionic focus to more easily overcome the power resistances of an outsider.

Divine minds of The Planes mantle could pinpoint the location of an outsider or extraplanar creature that was within range of their psychic aura. Additionally, the manifester and allies within the radius of their aura were more capable of overcoming spell and power resistances of outsiders.

Powers
Novice manifesters had greater ease traversing the Astral Plane, gaining the powers astral caravan and astral traveler. Manifesters of some experience could restrict planar movement with psionic dimensional anchor, force creatures back to their native plane with psionic dismissal, or travel to any plane with psionic plane shift. As a manifester progressed further they could enter the ethereal plane with psionic ethereal jaunt and summon a cerebrilith or sibyllic guardian to their aid with planar champion. Masters of this mantle obtained psionic etherealness, allowing them to bring other creatures with them into the ethereal.

## The Reward of Tomy

"The Reward of Tomy" was a play written in Kozakura that told a story of the first emperor Akimatsu Mori and the humble chef Sumitomo Tomy early in the nation's history.

Description
A noh play, it told the story in a stylized way and could be performed by geisha.

In the story, the newly ascended Emperor Akimatsu Mori decided to stay at the Nami No Hana (Crest of the Wave) inn on the night following the battle of Kyoki in . However, the master chef there was brother to a slain soldier of the army defeated at Kyoki and wanted revenge. The chef prepared the first emperor's celebratory dinner—the house specialty, raw tiger fugu and daikon (radish) sculpted to resemble a flying crane—with the poisonous fugu liver mixed in with the radish sauce on the crane's crest. But a sharp-eyed apprentice chef, Sumitomo Tomy, spotted something off with the food as it was served, rushed past the guards, and stopped Mori before he could take the deadly bite. The would-be poisoner was invited to dine with the emperor, and forced to eat his own cooking.

Afterward, Emperor Mori offered to elevate Tomy to noble status in recognition and gratitude, but Tomy explained that all Sumitomos were master chefs and changing his status would be a dishonor to the previous generations. He only wanted to finish his training as a chef and maybe one day own his own kitchen, as the founder of the Sumitomo family had dreamed for one of his descendants. The emperor understood and departed but later still wanted to give a recompense to the valorous and modest Tomy. He felt the land needed more chefs than daimyos anyway.

Therefore, the very day that Tomy finished his training, he was surprisingly arrested by a company of imperial soldiers at the emperor's command. They escorted him to Maeshi Province, Tomy's home, where the emperor had decreed the construction of two new roads and a grand new inn at their crossing. Outside, the captain of the company gave the keys to the bemused Tomy and explained the emperor had granted him proprietorship of the new inn and marked him as a master chef. Moreover, the inn would be always protected by an imperial decree punishing anyone who harmed the owner or violated its hospitality with a death sentence.Tomy named his new inn Doi no Fugu, "Inn of the Globefish", after the incident and went to work.

A year after, on the anniversary of the battle of Kyoki, Emperor Mori went to eat a dish of fugu prepared by Tomy.

History
"The Reward of Tomy" was one of the entertainments performed for guests by the geisha on staff following banquets at Doi No Fugu, such as Sumitomo Miko and Sumitomo Myoki.

In, members of the Ono Kumi ninja yakuza secretly took over the inn in order to intercept a band of adventurers and steal the relics of the extinct Seven Swords clan. As part of their elaborate ruse, Ono Minbu and Ono Heishiro posed as geisha and even performed "The Reward of Tomy" for the guests, even if it did mean men playing as women playing as men.

## Thaltar Glaervar

Thaltar Glaervar was a Red Wizard of Thay in the mid-14 century DR.

Appearance
He was shorter but heavier than Alustriel Silverhand.

Personality
Thaltar hedged much, and minded not to appear more confident than he was.

Abilities
He knew at least one spell that created a blazing light so bright it could distract even a Chosen of Mystra, akin to pyrotechnics. Another of his spells created a deadly black flame, which nullified some spells.  He also knew the manyjaws spell, though he changed it to use serpents; another of his spells created a silvery sword whose strike left a persistent spell-dampening field, making it a challenge to cast any spells. Another spell called a lash to his hand, and he could also cast a spell to animate ropes. He knew a form of telekinesis levitation, dancing lights and meteor swarm, which was his most powerful spell. He had some manner of sigil sewn into his clothes, which allowed him to unleash six different spells by merely speaking aloud certain words for each. Finally, he could use some magic to fetch objects in the vicinity, and he had at least one spell that sprayed acid over time, likely acid rain.

Possessions
His robes had his name written on them. He wore leather boots to meetings, and had an enchanted ring that could unleash a wall of force. Another ring allowed him to unleash a teleporting spell.

Relationships
He was part of a strange cycle-teleporting effect that allowed him to trade locations with the Waterdhavian merchant Auvrarn Labraster, but in return, he was bound to do the same whenever called on by the fellow Red Wizard Roeblen, with little warning time. This cycle had been forced upon him as part of his participation in an extensive cabal; linked into the same cycle were the Red Wizard Azmyrandyr and an especially large umber hulk. The red wizards were of Auvrarn Labraster's rank or higher. The cabal to which the Red Wizards belonged also boasted among its ranks the red wizards Skloon, Harkon, two Sharran priests, Speaker Amalrae, and a number of other Red Wizards.

He spent time together with a different cabal with the Red Wizards Iyrtaryld, Olorus, Dlamaerztus, Norlarram, Quaerlesz, and six others.

History
At some point, Thaltar Glaervar joined a cabal that, under direction from Halaster Blackcloak, took charge of numerous intrigues throughout Faerûn. One of the things that this cabal did was put him in a form of cycling teleportation together with two other Red Wizards, a Waterdhavian merchant, and one very big umber hulk.

In, Thaltar answered a call from Roeblen, who employed the teleporting link to swap himself out of a fight against Alustriel Silverhand and thus escape from Silverymoon, where he'd been summoned by a chain of linked teleports leading to Auvrarn Labraster, whom Alustriel believed to be hiding information regarding a murder. He left almost as soon as he arrived, barely casting a spell to dazzle the High Lady with bright light before executing his getaway, struck with a faceful of silver fire in return.

Later that year, while participating in a moot with other Red Wizards to discuss Iyrtaryld's newest development on the Hungry Mouth, they were assaulted by some manner of stone creature that slew most of them. Thaltar managed to escape, and came across a second Quaerlesz, who turned out to be the Simbul after he struck it with a black flame spell. He struck at her again and again, finishing her off with a meteor swarm that slew two apprentices, leaving only charred bones and a wand. He seized the wand and dissolved the bones in acid.

At his next meeting with the co-conspirators under Halaster Blackcloak, he learned of the deaeths of Roeblen and Azmyrandyr. Then he revealed his slaying of the Simbul, claiming it meant they were going to be attacked by the other five surviving Seven Sisters next; however, the wand revealed itself to be the Simbul, who unleashed some manner of spell-reflecting sphere on the room. The trapped conspirators used a veritable cornucopia of spells on the sphere trapping them; one of them, a ray of cutting force, took Thaltar in the chest, slaying him.

## The Hungry Mouth

The Hungry Mouth was a unique magic devised by the Red Wizard Iyrtaryld in the mid-to-late 14 century DR.

Effects
The spell created a moving portal that vacuumed everything around the target area, which could be all the way across Faerûn; its Thayvian creator intended to target the lands across the Raurin. Everything vacuumed into the portal was teleported to a place strongly implied to be in the vicinity of the caster. The caster could also be replaced while casting, handing over the task of maintaining concentration, so as to sustain the effect continuously rather than restart it.

History
In, the creator of the spell Iyrtaryld discussed it with a cabal of Red Wizards including the mages Olorus, Thaltar Glaervar, Quaerlesz, Dlamaerztus and Norlarram, alongside six others and himself. He announced a reduction in the rate of backlashes during handover between mages. There was some attempted discussion of what would happen if it sucked in a mage, or an active dangerous spell effect, but before that could be settled they were all assassinated by the Simbul.

## The Maedar's Widow

The Maedar's Widow was a shop in the Upper Trade Lanes of Skullport in the late 14 century DR.

Structure
The Maedar's Widow was a two-story building in good condition.

Services
The Maedar's Widow specialized in creating lifelike, one-of-a-kind statues, "captured" in stone rather than sculpted. The owner of the shop, a medusa named Morganis Andropoea, acquired able-bodied slaves from the Slavers' Market in the Lower Port, carefully attired them in elaborate garments and uniforms befitting their intended display, then positioned them in carefully curated poses. Once satisfied, she subjected them to her petrifying gaze, transforming them into flawless stone figures of eerie realism.

These sculptures were then meticulously crated and shipped to the halls and estates of the wealthy and indulgent, particularly in Waterdeep, where they commanded exorbitant prices due to their unsettling authenticity and craftsmanship. Her work has found particular favor among certain nobles who had taken to displaying these living sculptures as centerpieces in their collections, oblivious, or indifferent, to the grisly nature of their creation.

History
The Maedar's Widow was named in memory of Morganis's late husband, Holmyrr, a maedar slain nearly three decades ago by an adventuring party. Morganis fled to Skullport following his death and established her macabre trade in sculptures.

The Busy Gardener's Illustrated Guide to Gentle Magical Enhancements was one of the books that possessed some magic, to the Avowed's surprise. Its enchantments went out of control and started spewing living vines as well as unleashing a shambling mound onto the library and its guests. Tessalynde's group managed to slay the shambler and close The Busy Gardener's Guide, stopping the chaos. ## The Armoire of Queen Serenia of Mulhorand

The Armoire of Queen Serenia of Mulhorand was a unique and humble armoire that belonged to the wife of Pharaoh, Sorenhotep I, of the Second Empire of Mulhorand.

Description
Queen Serenia's Armoire was tiny, not what one expected from a cabinet that belonged to royalty. It was a relatively tiny chest made of the finest wood. Its construction and decoration were done with the highest levels of artistry.

History
The Armoire of Queen Serenia of Mulhorand dated back to the waning days of the Second Empire of Mulhorand. The kingdom's young Pharaoh, Sorenhotep I, was convinced that he needed a queen of beauty greater than any other mortal woman of the Realms. The Pharaoh sent messengers to all, even the farthest part of the world, in search of such a wife. One of the royal messengers returned with the story of the fey princess Serenia. Without hesitation, Sorenhotep organized a caravan to the princess's land and placed a Mulhorandi diplomat as its leader with five thousand soldiers, one hundred wizards, forty bards, dozens of wagons made from gold, cages full of animals from the royal zoo, mechanical wonders from the Mulhorandi workshops, truly a delegation to behold.

Serenia was not impressed by the wonders and lavish gifts sent her way. Many kings had the same treasures to brag about. Princess informed the Mulhorandi ambassador that only one thing could win her hand in marriage – if the king could present her the fabled unicorn of Ganathwood so the princess could ride on its back to the wedding. Sorenhotep consulted his royal magicians but was informed that no one could capture the beast; it was amazingly strong and fast, besting all hunters who had ever tried. Only a fair and pure maiden could distract the creature long enough for it to be harnessed. The Pharaoh ordered the kingdom's young maidens to be gathered and sent to Ganathwood, but months passed by, and none of the Mulhorandi girls were successful.

Princess Serenia was surprised to see the Mulhorandi diplomat return to her court with good news – the legendary unicorn was captured, but the princess had to travel to Ganathwood, where Sorenhotep kept the beast. Serenia complied and was greeted with no man, no soldier, just the forest. It did not take long for the fabled unicorn to present itself and lay its head on the princess's lap. Suddenly, the Mulhorandi soldiers leaped from their hiding and roped the unicorn.

Princess Serenia was outraged by the deception at first, but eventually came to a realization that the crafty Pharaoh did just what she asked of him and simply outwitted her. She agreed to the marriage and became Queen Serenia of Mulhorand.

In the, The Armoire of Queen Serenia of Mulhorand was displayed in Mintassan's Mysteries, a curio magic goods shop of Westgate. The history of Queen Serenia was attached to the armoire's knob, written on a small piece of paper.

The Pedestal of Jondar the Valiant was the lower part of what once was thought to be a statue of Jondar the Valiant, a paladin of Helm, who slew a medusa in the Starspire Mountains in the .

Description
The Pedestal of Jondar the Valiant was an old carved slab of stone that once held a statue on top of it. The block was plastered with moss and its sides were decorated with carvings of medusa heads.

History
After Jondar's heroic deed, slaying a medusa, her likeness was said to have been carved out of stone by the stonecutters' guild of Ithmong in or soon after 1217 DR. The statue was placed at the center of town atop a great fountain. With generations passing, details of the statue's creation became obfuscated, and her deeds in dealing with medusae forgotten. The statue of Jondar the Valiant remained atop the fountain, growing moss and collecting pigeon dung.

The Pedestal of Jondar the Valiant was all that was left from a statue after a mage named Mibbet the Meddler, in the, decided to cast the stone to flesh spell. It was just a whim, but the spell took hold, and the statue, now Jondar in flesh and blood, stepped down from the pedestal, thanked Mibbet, and walked off into the sunset.

In the, The Pedestal of Jondar the Valiant was displayed in the magic curio shop that belonged to Mintassan the Magnificent, a planeswalker from Westgate. Jondar's story, the statue's creation, and the paladin released from her stony prison were written on a plaque near the Pedestal.

## Thavverdasz

Thavverdasz was a powerful lich of the 13 century DR and the self-styled Harper King who played a key role in the events following the Harpstar Wars. He was once an ally of both the Cult of the Dragon and Harper bard Rundorl Moonsklan, though he ultimately betrayed them all in his bid for power.

Base of Operations
Thavverdasz dwelled in a cave on the edge of the Vast Swamp, within the Thunder Peaks north of Daerlun.

History
Before his rise as the Harper King, he was already allied with the Cult of the Dragon.

During the aftermath of the Harpstar Wars, the ambitious Harper bard Rundorl, in desperation after being betrayed by Szass Tam, sought out Thavverdasz to aid in intercepting the undead Harpers under Szass's control. Rundorl offered him the service of the Harpers and their hoarded magical treasures in exchange for help. Thavverdasz agreed—but promptly took over Rundorl's mind and assumed his hoped-for title of "Harper King" himself.

With Rundorl transformed into his undead servant, Thavverdasz took control of the reanimated Harpers and set out to subjugate the living ones. He manipulated the Cult of the Dragon into supporting his cause until he betrayed them as well, stealing a large cache of gems meant for the dracolich Khalahmongre.

In retaliation, the Cult rallied its forces, and Szass Tam—humiliated by how easily Thavverdasz had broken his control—sent a powerful magical simulacrum of himself to attack Thavverdasz's lair, now called the Court of the Harper King, in the . The battle between the two liches devastated the surrounding swamp as Thavverdasz's magical wards redirected Szass's spells outward, annihilating both undead Harper and Cultist forces. Eventually, Thavverdasz destroyed Szass Tam's magical projection using a potent magical item. The backlash disrupted Szass Tam's senses, leaving him incapacitated in Thay for years. In the aftermath, as Thavverdasz claimed victory, he proudly addressed the skull of a Harper he slew long ago—only for it to transform into the face of Elminster and explode. Severely weakened, Thavverdasz was destroyed when Elminster arrived in person, ending the lich's reign.The Grand History of the Realms, p. 125, instead has Szass Tam defeat Thavverdasz and Elminster defeat Szass Tam. This appears to be a misreading of the events detailed in The Code of the Harpers, p. 33.

## The Wailing Wench Tavern

The Wailing Wench Tavern was a spacious tavern and inn built in the Tyr's Eye plaza of the Blacklake District in the late 14 century DR.

Structure
The Wench a large horseshoe-shaped three-storied building with steeply pitched roofs and timber-framed walls. Its entrance was located at the inner side of the horseshoe's curve, the building's wings looming over it, forming a small courtyard. The building had multiple gabled roofs and dormer windows on all three floors. The tavern was easy to notice thanks to its external walls of plaster and wooden beams. The entrance was under a small awning with a sign displaying the tavern's name dangling above.

The tavern's front side was fenced with benches lining its walls.

Interior
The tavern's taproom was typical for the region. It featured stone-laden floors and walls. Several load-bearing stone columns were placed around the room with dinner tables, chairs, couches, and private booths. The walls were draped in tapestries depicting the Neverwintran Eye & Tears design.

History
Following the Shadow War of the, the Tyr's Eye plaza suffered a fire that destroyed several buildings that stood there as well as the city's mage school. The Wailing Wench Tavern was built in place of the torched businesses on the northeastern side of Tyr's Eye.

Inhabitants
Half-orcish paladin Grykk Bannersworn was one of the Wench's guests in 1374 DR. Some of the performers who graced the tavern with their shows included Finch the bard as well as Shymon and Scarbunkel.

## The Hallow-Halls

The Hallow-Halls, or The Small-Temples, was a scenic city block in the Altarside neighborhood of Ravens Bluff's Temple District, home to numerous small temples or shrines dedicated to deities of the elven, dwarven, halfling, and gnomish pantheons.The City of Ravens Bluff refers to the buildings as "temples", whilst Beautification Day and The Return use the term "shrines". Both of the names the block was known by were unofficial, though widely used.

Locations
The block was encircled by Manycoins Way to the north, Raven Way to the east, Crothmar's Lane to the west, and DeVillars Ride to the south.

Description
The small temples that filled the Hallow-Halls were of beautiful make, with smooth curving walls of stone. They had magical protections cast upon them. And at the heart of the block stood a splendidly well-kept grove of trees with a spring-fed pool in its center.

Inhabitants
The Hallow-Halls complex was a popular public space among elves, often quietly crowding it, taking in the atmosphere of the forest groves before moving on with their day.

Each of the temples were tended to by priests, such as Alysia Rosebud who oversaw the shrine of Hanali Celanil, Fiona Starlight a priestess of Sehanine Moonbow, and Jackie Fancytoes who oversaw the shrine of Sheela Peryroyl.

History
Sometime in the late 14 century DR, in the month of Uktar or "The Rotting", a cult dedicated to the dead power Moander and backed by the deity Ghaunadaur chose The Small-Temples to be the second site in their series of attacks with an experimental gas weapon that had been made near Dark Hollow. They narrowed it down to the shrine of the Seldarine, as they were rivals of Ghaunadaur. A Moanderite in green robes tried to enter the shrine, but was stopped at the door by temple guards. He chose to drop the vial there, unleashing the gas weapon and killing dozens of innocent Ravenians, as well as a nearby unit of City Watchmen that had rushed over to aid the temple guards. All exposed to the green gas were disintegrated, leaving behind no bodies.

A group of adventurers working for the Scout Rangers arrived shortly on the scene, alerted to the attack by the sounds of screaming and a panicking crowd. Most of the shrine's wooden entrance had been decimated, there were holes in the its ceiling, and one side of the complex had caved in due to disintegrated wooden pillars. The pillars displayed clean, smooth cuts from the gas. But overall, the shrine was still standing and not likely to collapse anytime soon, thanks to its stone make and magical wards. Alysia Rosebud stood transfixed at the sight of her Hanalian shrine, even as she stood the risk of being trampled by the throng of panicked people. The adventurers brought the priestess to her senses and consoled her, learning all that they could from her testimony.

Through further investigation of the scene the adventurers found the number of affects to imply over forty civilians people were disintegrated, the armor and weapons of six City Watchmen, two holy symbols of Corellon Larethian that had been dropped by the temple guards, and the holy symbols and personal affects of ten priests of various faiths. They also discovered, alongside the vial, a pin in the shape of the symbol of Moander, a right hand with an open fanged mouth in its palm.

## The Moonflame

The Moonflame was a grand temple dedicated to Selûne, the goddess of the moon, in the Temple District of Ravens Bluff.

Location
This temple stood in the Altarside neighborhood of Ravens Bluff's Temple District, taking up an entire city block close to Clearwater Harbor. It was bounded by MacIntyre Path, Morlgar's Ride, O'Kane Court, and Raven Way.False Prophecy describes the Moonflame as being located in the Uptown District, "in a garden next to the river" and "next to the river bridge". The river in question most likely refers to DeVillars Creek. While the artistic postermap included in Gateway to Ravens Bluff, the Living City (1989) does show the temple as being adjacent to the river, the more detailed map in The City of Ravens Bluff (1998) places both it and DeVillars Park much further away. Its main entrance faced Raven Way, along which it was directly across from DeVillars Park.

Structure
The original Moonflame was a circular building,It is unclear if the temple featured in Winter Weather Woes is supposed to be the old or new Moonflame. It features the glassteel domed roof the latter is known for, yet Mirial is still alive and that new building had not finished construction until after the Three Women War. Not to mention, neither buildings' floor plan lend credence to the idea of having a circular shape. constructed of white marble, with broad steps leading up to a portico entrance. It had a domed glassteel roof. And the colors navy blue and silver featured prominently throughout.

Construction of a new Moonflame was underway prior to the Three Women War, but it wouldn't finish until after the conflict. Its successor was a far larger and grander complex, a truly exquisite structure, topped with a dome and spires, it was considered by some to be one of the most beautiful human temples in the city. Its tremendous central dome was encircled by four smaller domes. All five domes had been constructed with the spell glassteel, making them both clear and incredibly tough. These domes granted those inside the temple a view of the moon and lit up in a spectacular way when moonlight hit them, creating a visual display that some referred to as "moonflame".

The exterior of the temple had a courtyard, whose wall was partially formed by the building itself. The yard took up an area measuring  wide and  in length. The temple's yard boasted an assemblage of standing stones with carved out holes. Angled mirrors were affixed high atop the temple walls to deflect beams of moonlight down and through the precisely arranged standing stones, directing the beams through their holes and down onto groomed patches of moss. The yard also had a series of evergreens, which added to its tranquil atmosphere, and a fountain near each street corner. These four fountains were distinguished from one another by each being carved to resemble one of the phases of Selûne: a full-moon, a crescent-moon, a half-moon, and a new-moon.

Interior

The original temple was a more modest structure, composed of twelve rooms and a large garden with a fountain. These rooms included a foyer, several bedchambers, a private bedchambers for the High Moonmistress, a healing ward with six cots, a kitchen and eating area, and a room where temple supplies were stored. It was decorated throughout with images of stars, the moon, and navigation devices. Within its main chapel the windows were arranged in such a way as to form a lunar calendar – one could determine the date by judging how Selûne's light shone on the floor. A small, but elegantly decorated sitting room was later added off of the main temple. It was bedecked in scenes of the nightsky, with each wall depicting a different quarter phase of Selûne.

The reconstructed Moonflame had a grand entrance hall, with walls bespoken in murals depicting historical events in the life of their goddess Selûne. The hall culminated in three sets of staircases, two smaller staircases that lead downstairs into the Hall of the Silver Moon and one larger staircase that lead to the temple's main floor. This hall acted as a dining room, but was also used for holding banquets and wedding receptions. On that same floor one could find the numerous sleeping quarters available to the public.

From the main floor one could move directly forward into the Chapel of the Moonflame, where church services were held. It was situated directly below the temple's central glassteel dome. This large room had a suitably big dedicated altar near its southern wall, benches and pews lining its eastern and western walls, marble flooring that seemed to give off a light glow even during daylight hours, and more murals depicting historic events in the life of Selûne. This included the ever famous mural of Selûne battling Shar. To the back of the hall were two antechambers, rooms wherein preparations were made for services, that also connected to the rearmost hallway around the living quarters of the temple's High Priests.

The hallways to the left and right of the Chapel of the Moonflame lead to the temple's several living quarters, The right hallway housed the quarters of the adventuring clergy, adventurers of Ravens Bluff who enrolled at Moonflame, whilst the left hallway housed the living quarters of the temple's permanent residents. Down the left hallway were also a common room for recreational activities and a small library. Each wing had only a single shared washroom. At the end of both hallways were doors that connected the singular hallway surrounding the rooms of the High Priests. This area of the temple was known as the West Wing.

The West Wing was off limits to all but the High Priests and certain powerful clergy. Besides offices and sleeping quarters, the wing housed a sacred artifact known as the Orb of Selûne, which promised protection so long as it was joined with the Moonflame. It sat upon an altar made of pure silver, though it was sturdy as adamantite, and chased with runes and inscriptions that spoke of the orb's value, Both the orb and its altar initially resided within the Chapel of the Moonflame, but were later moved to this more secure space.

The West Wing room the Orb of Seûne was stored within was secured by a silver-inlaid doorway, etched in runes and marked by a soft-glowing symbol of the moon. This always matched whatever Seûne's current phase was above Toril. The door was warded in magics that not only kept it in a locked state, but which would destroy any who touched it, save for the High Priests. Inside, the orb's altar was ringed by stone steps, topped with heavy carpeting for purposes of occasional prayer by those with the clearance to enter. A single steep skylight, warded with magic to fend off both intruders and the weather, gave view to the outside world. The room's walls were adorned in mosaics depicting the phases of Selûne, flanked by scenes depicting the story of the Orb's retrieval from the gem dragon Dektherissamin. As a last line of defense, four stone golems were stationed in the room. Each was sculpted in the likeness of one of the temple's High Priests and sat upon a stone pedestal in one of the room's four corners.

At some point in the late 14 century DR, the temple interior had a small grove of trees added to it, their growth limited only by the building's roof.

Services
The clergy could be asked to raise someone from death, though such spells usually carried a steep fee. The Moonflame also had sleeping rooms on its lower floor, available to the public at the cost of one copper piece per night. And on more than one occasion, individuals approached the Mooneflame's clergy for the purposes of curing them of lycanthropy, such as by paying a fee to have remove curse cast upon them.

Activities
The Moonflame was renowned for its parties, which it held at least every tenth day of the tenday, starting at dusk and possibly going for as late as the early light of dawn. As well as its luminous, green moonwine that some sailors partook a bit too much of. But by far their most popular celebration occurred during the winter solstice – on this longest night of the Calendar of Harptos many would hang wreathes of holly and burn bayberry candles, leaving them going until they snuffed themselves out. At night, which was known as "Alban Arthan", was when people would go attend the temple's yearly ceremony. According to some, this ceremony was one of the most beautiful to occur throughout the year. Beyond public celebrations, the clergy had two sacred rituals that were restricted to the faithful, called the Conjuring of the Second Moon and the Mystery of the Night.

Nightly worship services occurred either outside, within the temple's courtyard, or within the temple itself in the Chapel of the Moonflame. Both barefoot priestesses and lay worshipers would kneel for prayer, or dance in worship, atop the moonlit patches of moss in the temple's yard. Patrols of the City Watch typically maintained close observation of the temple yard at night for the purpose of keeping its thinly-clad clergy from harm. The duty was reportedly quite popular among Watchmen, receiving plenty of volunteers.

The temple also kept records of its goings on, but these were usually unavailable to those outside of the clergy.

Outside of the temple itself, members of the clergy ran a poor house in the city's Crow's End district, called the Hand of Selûne Charity Center.

When it came to rewarding adventurers who aided the church in some manner, one common method was to gift potions of moon-healing. Another was to grant them a "Favor of Selûne", redeemable at any later date. This favor guaranteed the recipient a choice between either receiving two moderate spells of their choice or having remove curse cast upon them.

Inhabitants
For much of its history the Moonflame was led by a high priestess called the High Moonmistress. In the late 14 century DR the temple went through several High Moonmistresses, including Starglitter, Mirial Moonsilver, Jenethra Mooncrown, and Arial Nightglow.

Arial Nightglow had previously served as the Chief Assistant to all of the aforementioned High Moonmistresses. And in 1366 DR, before her assassination, Starglitter had been preparing Arial to eventually start her own temple somewhere in the region.

Mirial was a very driven and popular leader, intent on expanding the influence of Selune in the Vast. Under her organizational skills the temple prospered and grew. She and her predecessor both had Grae Angell as a personal guard, who was deeply affected by his failure to defend Starglitter and continued to feel responsible for her death nigh on three years later.

The Moonflame saw a significant change in its leadership structure in the . Four silverstars went on a daring mission on behalf of Selûne and so pleased the goddess with their work that she decided all of them should be leader of the Moonflame. Each of them would represent a phase of Selûne and assume leadership of the temple during their specific quarter of Selûne. These four leaders were Aric Moonstone, High Initiate of the Full Moon; Amanda Redmoon, High Initiate of the Crescent Moon; Valas Stargazer-Blackmantle, High Initiate of the Half Moon; and Daren of Selûne, High Initiate of the New Moon. However, since the Moonflame's leadership was unstable, changing every few days, Arial Nightglow essentially continued to act in a leadership role. Later that same year Aric accidentally underwent a magical change of sex and took on the name Alessia. She tried to pass herself off as a completely new priestess, going to the effort of having a simulacrum made of her former male-self.

Under this leadership the priestess Arakha Dunsoun held the position of Moonhand. She was encharged with maintaining the peace and tranquility of the temple grounds, as well as the safety of its clergy.

One of the few notable residents of the Moonflame that weren't members of the clergy was Starhope, the orphaned child of a priestess. She was raised in a pampered fashion by the temple's clergy and looked after the younger children in the Moonflame. She also tutored under Aric Moonstone to one day be a cleric herself.

History
At some point in the early 14 century DR, Lady Lauren DeVillars sponsored the construction of a shrine to Waukeen within the heavily Selûnite populated Harbor District. The Moonflame's priests opposed and voted against the plans, feeling that they held domain over the waterfront district, but they were overruled by the city's Clerical Circle. In an effort to mollify their concerns, Lady DeVillars decided to also sponsor the construction of an observatory for the Church of Selûne on the Hammerfell Heights. Around that time a traveling Selûnite by the name of Novak arrived in Ravens Bluff and was outraged over the compromise. He decided to sabotage the construction of the Waukeenar shrine and fake a prophecy, foretelling of his plans, impersonating a local soapbox preacher named Blind Billy. Some of the workers involved went on to speculate that Blind Billy was working on behalf of the Moonflame and the clergy in turn were possibly behind the acts of sabotage going on. Meanwhile, Waukeenar High Priest Galvan Sharpeyes was unwilling to believe the Moonflame was responsible.

When High Priestess Starglitter was confronted with these accusations by a group of adventurers, she made a rare daylight appearance to issue a public statement that the Moonflame had no involvement with either the acts of sabotage or Blind Billy. She denounced his prophecies as ramblings, unsupported by prayers and spells she used to divine Selûne's will. She then offered each of the adventurers healing prayers in return for putting the prophecy matter to rest and gifted each of them a silver medallion in the shape of a crescent moon.

In the, in the month of Kythorn, a cult of Cyricists established a temple within the sewers of Ravens Bluff. Six months later Chief Prelate Sirrus Melandor and then-head of the Moonflame, Starglitter, were close to discerning the location of their temple and determined to remove them from the city. After learning of this, Cyricist Micarlin Narklath summoned an assassin spirit to murder Starglitter on the night of Uktar 28. She tried to fend it off with flame strike, but to no avail. At that same time her Chief Assistant, Arial Nightglow, was busy preparing for the evening services.

An hour or two later Arial discovered Starglitter's body. She quickly sought the scrying pool in Starglitter's room to contact High Priestess Wyndra Syrylstone, head of Selûne's main temple in the Eastern Heartlands. With the Feast of the Moon fast approaching, Wyndra urged Arial not to alarm the other Selûnites, as the festival required a high priestess and she wanted to ensure her replacement's safety. She authorized Arial to hire a group of adventurers to discretely handle the person responsible, paying them no more than 1,250 GP each, and if they failed she was to contact the City Watch. Arial wasted no time in sending out novice priestesses to find adventurers willing to help. Within an hour a group of adventurers were found and brought before Starglitter's corpse, covered with a large heavy blanket. After investigating the scene and questioning priests within the temple, the adventurers head out into the night, armed with a prayer from Arial and a powerful wand of dispel magic on loan from Wyndra.

The adventurers managed to uncover the Cyricists and their plot to murder Sirrus Melandor next. They engaged in an extraneous battle within the sewers, ultimately coming out triumphant. Hours before they would arrive back at the Moonflame, a mage in the employ of Wyndra teleported Starglitter's replacement to the temple. When the adventurers returned, late-night mass was just at its end and it was a few hours until dawn. They were greeted by Arial, who brought them inside and introduced them to the new High Priestess, Mirial Moonsilver.

Over the next three years Mirial worked to expand the influence of the Church of Selûne in the region, building up its temple and making repeated requests to Wyndra to send her more clergy to aid in running the Moonflame.

Before the Three Women War kicked off, the Selûnite clergy and the city's population of lay worshipers grew, culminating in pressure to construct a larger temple that was eventually met. However, with the advent of the war the clergy as a whole were unable to complete and occupy the new Moonflame.
Three Women War Period
In the, Wyndra Syrylstone sent the priestess Katrina Star away from Calaunt to train under Mirial Moonsilver in Ravens Bluff, feeling that she showed great promise. While en route to the city, Katrina was kidnapped and tortured by a Sharran priest, who took advantage of her arachnophobia. However, unbeknownst to the Sharran, the spiders he was using carried the curse of lycanthropy and would tranform Katrina into a werespider. Katrina slew her captor and, her mind twisted into a lawful evil state by the curse, continued her journey to Ravens Bluff with an insidious notion of infecting the Moonflame's clergy.

Over the next three months Katrina would enter the bed chambers of slumbering priests on nights of a full moon, sedate them with strong herbal mixtures, and leave the infected to believe they were simply experiencing strange identical nightmares every time they transformed. She especially targeted the specialty priests among the clergy, as silverstars had better control over lycanthropy transformations. By the month of Uktar, several of the clergy were infected and under Katrina's sway. Twelve people had died from attacks by the werespiders, either outside the temple or near the Hand of Selûne Charity Center. In every instance the victims' bodies were horribly mutilated, evidently from being attacked by a beast. Concerned by the rash of nightmares among her clergy, the string of attacks, and the fast approaching Feast of the Moon falling on the night of a full moon, Mirial decided to hire a group of adventurers to investigate the matter.

Due to the Moonflame's ongoing projects and the Three Women War raging in the background, the temple's funds were tight. All Mirial could offer the adventurers were moonstones from her private collection, worth 500 gold pieces. After receiving testimony from her bodyguard Grae, the adventurers left to investigate Mirial's assembled list of witnesses to the attacks. On the Feast of the Moon the adventurers were invited back to Moonflame to attend a "night stalk" ritual and they arrived just as dusk was closing over Ravens Bluff, the clergy assembled in the main chapel. The adventurers informed Mirial all that they had learned over the course of their investigation before she bid them to follow her into the garden.

The clergy walked in a line two abreast, Mirial at the forefront, each carrying a bowl of wine or milk from the chapel, down the hall into the dining room, and out to the temple gardens. They placed these bowls upon an altar and begin a chorus of chants. As Selûne's silvery light rose above the garden walls and down onto the clergy, their singing became cut off by anguished cries as they began transforming into werespiders. This included the likes of Ed Thrum, Troy Yacuk, and Vera Wingard. As the transformations were underway Mirial quickly cast Selûne's choice, hoping the quest spell would allow at least a few of her clergy to maintain control of their bodies, but was immobilized in a beam of moonlight as she maintained it. When the last of the werespiders fell, one of Selûne's Shards step forth from the moonlight enveloping Mirial. The shard took the form of a lovely girl, seemingly no older than 16 years of age, garbed in the plain brown robes of an acolyte of the church and with hair that hung down to her waist. The beam of moonlight disappeared shortly behind her. Mirial collapsed to the ground and the infected clergy began to transform back, their lycanthropy cured by the shard. When Mirial came to she thanked the adventurers for their help and ordered that all the fallen priests be buried among the unfaithful in the City Cemetery.

In the, on Eleint 21, the day of the holiday Remembrance Day, a group of Talassans assaulted the Moonflame with the explicit purpose of assassinating High Priestess Mirial, or more ambitiously the destruction of the temple itself before sundown. The Talassans, composed of both clerics and fighters, were led by Thunderhips, a Lliiran paladin who had fallen from grace and taken up worship of Talos. Their lightning attacks brought down a great explosion of fire and smoke, creating four large holes in the temple's roof and attracting the attention of nearby adventurers, whom included the likes of Andrews Womack. A significant portion of the damage was dealt by Thunderhips himself, using several spells and spell scrolls, including unholy words. By the time the adventurers arrived to intervene the Moonflame's defenders had been pushed back into the temple proper. And the priestess Auburn Bright was rallying her fellow Selûnites against the Talassans.

Even with the adventurers' aid in fending off the Talassans, the Moonflame's casualties from the attack were severe. Numerous clergy were dead and even more were missing. A number of Selûnites were able to be brought back to life thanks to scrolls and items that had been stored away within the temple's vaults, but fourteen priestesses and paladins remained dead, including Mirial's bodyguard Grae Angell. Mirial herself was deemed dead at the hands of Thunderhips. Last seen battling Talassans from the temple roof, her body was never recovered during the efforts to dig out the upper floors in search of survivors. Following this, temple services were scheduled to occur on the next full moon, whilst a memorial to the slain clergy was to be held and blessed during the next new moon. In the weeks following the attack, the Selûnites were reluctant to speak of the tragedy in anything but veiled terms.

In Mirial's absence, Jenethra Mooncrow acted as the temple's High Priestess. She would die two months later on one of the church's holy day ceremonies, when several members of the clergy were possessed by some foul magic and transformed into creatures that attacked the Selûnites gathered, lay worshipers and priestesses alike. The incident was reported on by the Ravens Bluff Trumpeter, who had scarce information on what went down, save some sources that claimed there were at least eight fatalities among the clergy.

As the war continued to rage on, over twenty more Selûnite priests and paladins lost their lives, including the likes of Rowel and Mary. By the end of the Three Women War, the old Moonflame had been rendered barely fit for use and was torn down.

Post-War Period
By the end of the war, the highest ranking priestess left alive was Arial Moonglow, thus she was forced to take up the role of leadership for the beleagured temple.

Arial inducted a number of likely novices into her sundered clergy. Around 1371 DR, a number of evergreen saplings were planted around the Moonflame. Also during that year a terrorist group called the Circle of Four was wreaking havoc among the temples of Ravens Bluff. After overtaking the temples of temples of Lliira, Torm, and Tyr with the combined aid of Cyricists, Talassans, and Talontar they planned to do the same to the rest of the city's temples, including the Moonflame. This incited people forming long lines outside of the city's remaining temples, including the Moonflame.

In the, the temple saw the enstatement of its four High Initiates of the Moon. That same year, the city's Temple of Sune was destroyed in a battle between avatars of Sune and the archdevil Glasya. While efforts were underway to construct a new Palace of Passion, the Moonflame offered refuge to the Sunite clergy, giving them lodging in many of the temple's quarters.

Continued clashes within Ravens Bluff saw further damage dealt to the temple, though some sort of protective magic seemed to be mitigating some of that potential damage. Rumors abounded that it was the will of Selûne herself protecting the temple.

Sometime later on Flamerule 20, when the Moonflame was under the leadership of Darin of Selûne and festivities were underway for the Midsummer's Festival, an extraplanar trader from Sigil named Tehtravese hired the powerful, cunning rakshasa Maharajah Lord Terrax to break into the temple and steal the Orb of Selûne, offering him in return control over werepanthers and weretigers. At the same time, a nefarious group called the Cabal of the Moon's Blood was planning to trash the festivities. With the help of his insider sources, Tehtraverse was able to coordinate his robbery to coincidence with this attack.

Chaos rang throughout the Temple District's crowded streets as weretigers of the Cabal attacked City Watchmen and the clergies of Selûne, Helm, and Lathander. At the Moonflame itself, the Cabal brought about many casualties, providing just the distraction Terrax needed to steal the Orb of Selûne. Utilizing a ring of spell storing, charged with the spell disintegrate, he cut out a deep, perfectly circular hole atop the surface of the altar to remove the Orb. Shortly after the theft, the metal of the altar and the glow given off by its runes both began to darken. When the clergy were alerted to the presence of two corpses on the northeast lawn, identified as priests who normally guarded the West Wing, panic began to strike. They hurried down the Chapel of the Moonflame and back into the Orb's secure room. There they discovered its stone golems were destroyed and the Orb nowhere to be seen. Despair, rage, and further panic overtook the clergy at the news of its theft. But even more surprising was what came next.

An acolyte announced that a small group of Sharrans had been walking through the Temple District, healing those injured by the Cabal's attack, and eventually made their way to the Moonflame's doorstep. Led by a Nightseer named Jesibelle, they sought an audience with High Priest Darin. Jesibelle spoke of having been sent by the goddess Shar herself to render unto them aid through information. She then provided to a group of adventurers that had accompanied Derin a map of Sarbreen, marked with the location of where Tehtraverse was holding an auction for the Orb of Selûne.

Traveling down into the lower depths of Sarbreen, fighting all manner of agents of evil organizations and faiths, the adventurers eventually managed to catch up to Tehtravese. He was standing in a magically dark cavern, in the company of Galatheron, a deep dragon who had came a long way to purchase the Orb. Tehtravese expounded about having been instrumental in the Selûnites' initial recovery of the Orb from the horde of Dektherissamin. He gave his reasoning for stealing as being twofold, just to see if it could be done and because the Selûnites had never paid him for his aid. He then offered them the change to bargain for its return, demanding half of their magical wealth as payment. Regardless of whether they agreed to this or not, Galatheron engaged the adventurers in combat.

When the adventurers vanguished the deep dragon, the darkness spells covering the cavern they were in dissipated, revealing a small portion of Galatheron's horde to surround them. They then noticed on the back of the Sharran's map was a drawing, faintly resembling the cavern in which they stood. turn with the Orb and be hailed as heroes. With no means of pursuing the evil individuals that had gotten away, the adventurers followed their map to the surface. When they returned they initially brought the Orb to its previous altar, but after no reaction occurred they took it to the altar within the Chapel of the Moonflame. There a latticework of pure silver manifested out of thin air and joined the Orb of Selûne to the altar.

The altar began to morph, taking on the form of two silver disks between the Orb, with bars of silver attaching and supporting one above the other. A hole then opened in the upper disk and the bars between them unfurled, leaving the upper disk to resemble Selûne's current phase. The goddess then spoke to the Moonflame's High Priests, telling them she wished for the adventurers who had rescued it to touch the Orb and receive her guidance. Darin of Selûne spoke to the adventurers, "I understand the sacrifice and risk you all took for the return of the Orb. I have wished to find a way to reward you, and the Lady has shown me her will . . . You will each be allowed to bath yourselves in the power of the Orb, and gain whatever the Lady wishes." Those who chose to partake of the offer received from Selûne a powerful vision of their destiny and were left marked by a permanent, silver glowing tattoo in the shape of the moon.

## The Boar with Black Tusks

The Boar with Black Tusks was the most noteworthy inn of the village of Noanar's Hold in the 14 century DR.

Structure
It was a stout, but long log building, stretched over rolling hills. It sat beneath the shade of old, sturdy shadowtops.

Interior
The overall conditions of the Boar were relatively the same as the other inns of Noanar's Hold. Its rooms included a common dining room, a bar, a kitchen, a bathing area, and a total of forty two guest rooms.

Much of the floors were furnished in worn rugs to keep one's feet warm, some of which looked to be old tapestries depicting northern hunting scenes that had been unfortunately cut up in order to make the tapestries fit into the hallways. The furniture, though stout and comfortable, were an eclectic mixture.

The Boar's well known steamy bathes were unisex and numbered five in total, with three being hot water baths and two being cool water baths. These baths were all made of copper, sunk into the floor, and had seat ledges inside of them to allow up to eight guests to sit comfortably. On any given day, at least one of the hot baths usually had scented oils available.

Atmosphere
The Boar's interior offered a rather cozy atmosphere. The services of its housemaids were notably courteous and timely.

The tremendous meals the inn offered often left diners falling asleep in the common dining roam, groaning over the quantity of food consumed, or staggering to their bedrooms for rest.

Services
A night at one of the Boar's guest rooms cost 4 gold pieces, with that payment also covering the guest's bath, meal, stabling, and one use of the inn's clothes-mending & laundry service. Choosing to forgo these amenities would not yield a discount. The inn offered no tenday staying rate. Feed for stabled creatures carried a separate 5 copper piece charge per mount. Additional uses of the inn's clothes-mending & laundry service cost a stiff 1 to 3 gp per garment. And food was not allowed to be taken into the guest rooms.

The inn kept a number of outer-clothes on stock to loan out to guests in cases when their clothing were either drying after a hunt or inappropriate for hunting. These included high boots, warm woollen overtunics, and weather-cloaks. Additionally, the Boar's many housemaids offered escort services, typically charging around 40 to 60 gp for a night of company.

The Boar's provender was identical to those of the other inns of Noanar's Hold. For those not staying at the inn, a meal cost a flat rate of 4 gp. For guests their meal included a carafe or pitcher of whatever drink the guest preferred. Additional drinks cost either 1 silver piece, if the desired drinking vessel was a glass or tankard, or 1 gp if the container was a bottle.

The meals on offer were always wild game, accompanied by cheese, pots of smoked and spiced river fish, and round loaves of hard, black nutbread. These salty fish mixtures ground together a variety of different fish that were old and gave off a strong odor. While the wild game on offer could vary day to day, courses usually followed a set pattern.

The first course of a meal was always fowl, accompanied by cabbage and some other greens. This would be followed by some form of small bodied local game, such as a fox, rabbit, or ground rodent. This typically was either cooked in a red wine or served with a white sauce. The third course was always some type of unusual game, like a beaver, wolf, or even manticore. This was followed by the primary meats of the meal, which were either bear, elk, or owlbear. The meal would at last be concluded with some form of jellies – of the flavors cranberry, mint, and sloeberry – a whole roasted boar, whose tusks were painted black in emulation of the inn's name, and steaming trays of meat that had been cooked in a thick gravy derived from the drippings of all the prior meals that the kitchen had prepared.

For diners on the go, the inn offered sack luncheons for 3 gp a piece. These consisted of a cold version of the eveningfeast, wrapped up in some pieces of old cloth and stuck inside a canvas sack.

Defenses
The inn had a strict ban on all manner of spellcasting. Anyone caught breaking this prohibition would be kicked out. This rule ostensibly existed for the purposes of preventing fires and other mayhem from unfolding in the Boar.

History
When travel writer Volothamp Geddarm had a brief visit to Noanar's Hold in 1365 DR, The Boar was the only inn of the hold's four that he had time to take in and commit his thoughts to in Volo's Guide to the North. Within the confines of that book, Volo would relay that Elminster had confirmed the Boar's infamous legend and his claim that the tale's anonymous mage was in fact one of the Hunt Lords.

Rumors & Legends
The Boar was famous for a grisly legend surrounding it, that told of a visiting adventurer who recognized one of their fellow guests as a former colleague and wizard that owed him coins. The man got confrontational, demanding the payment he was owed for quite some time. The guest responded by using spells to paralyze and polymorph the aggressor into a boar. The tale concluded with the guest having the polymorphed aggressor cooked and served at the end of the inn's evening meal in place of another boar.

Additionally, there were rumors that the Boar's various furnishings originated from a number of old, over-grown keeps across the High Forest, built by wizard lords in the immediate centuries following the Netherese Empire's fall. Some of these stories further talk of hidden treasure from those old keeps, tucked away in vaults beneath trapdoors or accessible only by secret passageways in certain rooms. These treasures were mostly said to be strange magical items that struck fear in their scavengers. By and large, these rumors were primarily spoken of in the city of Waterdeep.

Inhabitants
The Boar, like the rest of Noanar's Hold's inns, was collectively owned by the Horn Lords, a council of wizards that ruled over the village. Many, including visitor Volothamp Geddarm, suspected that the true purpose of their prohibition on spellcasting was to ensure that the Horn Lords didn't have to worry about opposition.The housemaids that worked in the Boar were likewise employees of all four inns, divvying their time between them.

## The Mortar and Pestle

The Mortar and Pestle was an apothecary and magical supply shop in the Central Port of Skullport in the late 14 century DR.

Structure
The Mortar and Pestle was a one-story building in fair condition.

Services
The Mortar and Pestle was recognized as one of the most dependable sources for spell components and potion reagents within Skullport. The shop also offered related magical services and engages in limited trade of arcane goods.

The shop maintained a broad inventory of material components for spellcasting and created both magical and non-magical potions and elixirs. Additional services included the scribing of protective scrolls, with a minimum turnaround time of three days, and the purchase of rare or unusual items potentially useful to spellcasters. A posting at the entrance listed specific items currently sought by the shop, along with the bounties offered for their delivery. All transactions were subject to negotiation; the staff frequently engaged in barter, exchanging potions for potions, scrolls for scrolls, or items for services.

The most frequently requested service was the identification of magical items recovered from Undermountain. This service was offered at a cost of 150 gold pieces per item, in addition to the required purchase of a 100 gold piece pearl necessary for the spell’s casting. The shop provided no guarantees regarding the accuracy of identification and offered no refunds under any circumstances. If an item was discovered to be cursed and the curse subsequently binded to the identifying wizard, the client was responsible for arranging and funding the necessary removal by a qualified cleric or wizard.

Inhabitants
The Mortar and Pestle was owned by Ruuth.

## The Wizards' Workbook

The Wizards' Workbook, also known simply as The Workbook, was a famous spellbook containing original spells devised by some of Faerûn's most notable wizards.

Description
There were no reliable accounts of The Workbook's appearance, although it was believed that it was a bound volume with no inscriptions on the cover.

Contents
Accounts of the book's contents varied, leading some to speculate that more than one so-called Wizards' Workbook had been created. Those spells that were attributed to the book by Elminster himself were Archveult's skybolt, Caligarde's claw, dismind, Laeral's dancing dweomer, Spendelard's chaser, Tasirin's haunted sleep, and Tulrun's tracer.

History
The Workbook (or maybe Workbooks) had been compiled in Myth Drannor sometime between the, and the . The spells were curated by a powerful archmage known as the Mentor Wintercloak, leader of the famed Seven Wizards who taught at the Incanistaeum school of magic. He personally tested the spells produced by the school's pupils, and included those that met with his approval into The Workbook. Those who received the honor of having a spell added to the book were said to include Archveult Tattercloak, Caligarde, Laeral Silverhand,Laerel Silverhand was not born until after the dissolution of the Seven Wizards, and so could not have been one of the pupils who contributed to The Workbook. This could be considered an error committed by Elminster when communicating the spells, or it could be the result of retcons. The first mention of The Workbook and its contents appeared in Dragon Magazine Issue #69, predating TSR's acquisition of the Forgotten Realms by several years. Spendelarde, Tasirin, Tulrun, and potentially Khelben Arunsun or the Mentor himself.

The Workbook eventually found its way into the hands of adventurers who sold it to the sage Flamsterd of Waterdeep. The sage grew rich by copying and selling several of the book's spells, and used this money to buy his own island in the Moonshae Isles where he moved with his apprentices. While living there, he copied the entirety of the book into his personal diaries, which he then shared with his good friend Elminster.

In the, Flamstered became fed up with his squabbling apprentices and, seeking peace and privacy to continue his development of new spells, he transported his tower and the surrounding penninsula to the bottom of the sea in a great eruption that left many (including Elminster) believing he was dead. A common theory was that a former buyer of his spells had deduced that he held the full Wizards' Workbook, and had killed him for it. The Workbook was likewise believed to have been destroyed.

Flamsterd would not reemerge for several decades, and in the meantime, Elminster saw fit to share the secrets of a number of the spells that had been shared with him. The copies of the spells sold by Flamsterd also remained in circulation around Faerûn, and around the 1340s DR, Flamsterd's diaries were published as The Moonshae Chronicles.

## The Forgotten Realms Wiki Presents Juniper's Companion to Venturesome Cookery

The Forgotten Realms Wiki Presents Juniper's Companion to Venturesome Cookery is a cookbook and sourcebook written, illustrated, and compiled by members of the Forgotten Realms Wiki team, Artie Pavlov, Brad McGrath, Jason William Labonte, Alex D. Paul, Iqarus, Chloe Grey, and Abby "Epikowl" Schreiber, based on the Juniper's Companion to Venturesome Cookery cooking blog by Artie Pavlov. It includes new and revised recipes from the Forgotten Realms; cooking tips and explanations for beginners; classic and homebrewed Realmslore; short fiction; illustrations and photographs; and spells and magical items using the 5-edition  ruleset. It also features a foreword and new lore by Forgotten Realms creator Ed Greenwood, a column by fellow Realms writer Steven E. Schend, cover art by 5-edition D&D artist Brian Valeza, and lyrics and lore by musician Elizaveta. It was released on Dungeon Masters Guild and DriveThruRPG on July 23, 2025.

Description

Juniper's Companion to Venturesome Cookery is styled as a leather-bound scrapbook by Juniper Churlgo, a halfling wizard adventurer and chef of the Churlgo Cheese family business based outside Daggerford, written by Artie Pavlov. This has been edited, annotated, and compiled for publication by gnome editor Monoselic Wordwrangle of Procampur, written by Brad McGrath. It features a variety of recipes and cooking advice, together with columns of lore on the locales, foods, and characters of Faerûn and beyond; collected articles and short fiction; sketches, artworks of foods, and maps; and notes on magical items and spells. It's all told in a friendly, informal manner (Juniper) or a dry, verbose one (Monoselic) with only occasional disputes between author and editor, all on aged paper with wine stains, coffee rings, and other suspicious marks retained.

It takes inspiration from the Volo's Guide series of sourcebooks from 2 edition and the graphic design of Forgotten Realms sourcebooks of 3 edition. No AI software was used in the writing of text or in the creation of artworks, though some photographs were cleaned with the assistance of AI-based tools.

Contents
With over 280 pages, the cookbook is divided into nine chapters: Introduction, Morningfeasts, Highsunfeasts, Eveningfeasts, Last Kisses, Smallbites, Breads, Manyslakes, and the Appendix, as well as the Foreword. Spread over these, the book presents 61 dishes, each with recipes for main dishes, sides, sauces, breads, and more, for a total of over 120 distinct recipes, with many more suggested variations and serving ideas. Seven of these dishes are exclusive to the cookbook and others are revised or updated from the blog. Each dish is accompanied by an introduction placing it in the Forgotten Realms setting, color photographs of the finished dishes and key stages of preparation, sidebars explaining cooking terms and techniques, other sidebars giving new and existing Realmslore, and footnotes from the editor giving additional tips, lore, and commentary. Interspersed are maps excerpted from the Forgotten Realms Campaign Setting 3rd edition poster map by Todd Gamble, Dennis Kauth, and Robert Lazzaretti with full-color illustrations of foods by Abby "Epikowl" Schreiber and other full-page artworks. Throughout the text are links to the Forgotten Realms Wiki to provide more background lore.

The Foreword by Ed Greenwood gives an introduction and assortment of Realmslore.

The Introduction presents a preface giving an overview of the book, an article on the culinary history of Faerûn, Steven E. Schend's column on the culture of halflings in Tethyr, and an article from the editor giving advice to fellow novice cooks. This is followed by lists of gluten free, vegetarian, and vegan recipes and an index of cooking notes in the book.

Morningfeasts covers the breakfast dishes, with Akabar Bel Akash's Trailside Gruel; Arrabarran Stuffed Fish; Baked Stirge on Toast; Chondathan Honey Cakes; Fendarl's Gate Morningfeast; Fryplate; Goldenstars; Illistyl Elventree's Morningfeast; Mint-Wine Sausages; and Sembite Bread Pudding.

Highsunfeasts gives the midday meals, with Blood Sauce and Beer-Battered Fishfry; Blushing Mermaid's Seaweed Stew; De'Arnise Boar Dumplings; Forester's Tarts; Gurneth's Goblet Ginger Shrimp; Kalath Smoked Fish Tarts; Kozakuran Dumplings; Leek Bread and Potato-Leek Soup; Tantran Baeranth; and Waterdhavian Cashew Soup.

Eveningfeasts presents the main meals: Alisanda's Asa Wat; Ashaba Trout; Baldurian Seafood Stew; Beef and Oysters Barnabas with Marsember Beets; Black Adder Stew; Bowl of Hares; Bustards; Lomatran Baked Beans; Luiren-Style Lamb Meatballs, Chessentan Lamb Meatballs, and Lambtails; and Roasted Pork Loin from Bargewright Inn with Cabbage & Greens from Noanar's Hold.

Last Kisses offers a selection of desserts and sweet snacks: Elfin Sponge; Endevver Buns; Hangman's Noose; Poppyseed Buns; Ravenaar Kaeth Cake; Silvaeren Cinnamon Pizza; The Silver Wink Milk Jelly; Sword Mountains Spice Cakes; Thayvian Walnut Pastry; and Turmishite Apple and Bloodberry Pie.

Smallbites includes a variety of snacks, mini-meals, and handfoods, with Ankhapuran Street Noodles; Calishite Pistachio Pizza; Dale Cheese; Greengrass Onion Cakes; Greensplatter in a Cheese Bowl; Feldepost's Cucumber Buns; Spread Bread; Talyth; Tethyrian Herb Pizza; and Tonguelash Dinner.

Finally, the Breads chapter covers Blackbread; Hin Sunflower Seed Buns; Nutbreads and Turmishian Onion & Chive Soup; Sembian Meatbread; and Sugarbread, while Manyslakes presents several beverages both alcoholic and not: Flaming Gullet; Kvas and Rashemaar Summer Quaff; The Moon's Head Brace; Tangled Trees Slake; and The Walking Furniture.

The book concludes with an Appendix presenting a range of cooking- and food-themed magics, with twelve spells and eighteen magic items updated to 5 edition rules; a final eveningfeast dish, Thaevor Potatoes, from the editor; a short story; and the lyrics of a song, "Echoes of the Chosen" by Elizaveta, released separately by the artist on Bandcamp.

History
The book began life with the popular Juniper's Companion to Venturesome Cookery blog by Artie Pavlov, who in November 2022 began creating recipes inspired by foods and drinks seen in Forgotten Realms novels, games, and sourcebooks and posting them to the Forgotten Realms Wiki. The blog was from the point of view of halfling wizard Juniper Churlgo. Juniper herself began as a player-character in the Legacy of the Green Regent D&D campaign run by Brad McGrath for fellow wiki editors since September 2021 (the campaign regrettably went on hold while creating this book). The book began production in June 2024.

## The Sword of Myrloch Vale

The Sword of Myrloch Vale was a legendary artifact that was said to have been created by the fey of the Myrloch lake in the Moonshae Isles, long before the 13 century DR.

Description
The Sword of Myrloch Vale was a beautifully crafted light longsword. It had a unique and unmistakable design, making it appear to be unearthly and very old.

Powers
It was a longsword that was swung with a greater speed than most similar weapons. In addition to its feather-light design, the blade possessed a potent +3 enchantment that made the weapon more deadly and that guided the wielder's hand towards the target. As such, The Sword of Myrloch Vale could damage creatures that were otherwise invulnerable to non-magical weapons. The blade also imbued the wielder's mind with unprecedented creativity, sensitivity, as well as knowledge of lore. When The Sword's true power was unlocked, it greatly increased the creativity and lore knowledge of the wielder even further than before, and boosted their charisma, making it a perfect weapon for a bard or a minstrel. Lastly, the magics that permeated The Sword of Myrloch Vale made the weapon impossible to wield by creatures of evil and malicious nature.

History
According to the legend of the Sword, it was forged with the help of fae creatures of the Moonshae Isles. It was believed that the creation took place in the depths of the cold waters of Myrloch, the lake at the center of the Isle of Gwynneth.

The only documented wielder of the blade was a half-elven bard named Daen Winterbrush. Some said that the bard found the blade by accident, but once it touched his hand, Daen was blessed with extraordinary creativity and sensitivity to the world and everything else that surrounded him. Daen's travels with The Sword of Myrloch Vale in his possession lasted for forty years, and the bard's artistic output made Daen known as the creator of some of the most unique and haunting melodies in all of Faerûn.

It was said that Daen Winterbrush's travels ended in a fit of powerful melancholy when he became disillusioned after witnessing misery and oppression. The fae smiths who created The Sword of Myrloch Vale welcomed the bard into their home in Myrloch. The Sword then remained lost until the late 13 century DR.

In the, The Sword of Myrloch Vale was found in the stock of Conlan's Smithy in the town of Kuldahar, nestled in the Spine of the World mountains. The powerful blade's true magic was still dormant and still needed to be discovered. It was believed that a group of adventurers sought out The Ballad of Daen Winterbrush, an unfinished work of the long-dead bard. They sang the ballad over the Sword, possibly with the help of Telanis of the Severed Hand or Murdaugh of Lonelywood, and conversed with Daen Winterbrush's ghost, which was tortured by his unfinished masterpiece. Once the adventurers finished the bard's work, he was allowed to rest once more, and the true power of The Sword of Myrloch Vale was unlocked.

At some point before his death in the, the white dragon Ingeloakastimizilian, also known as Icingdeath, the mate of Ixbillailzakzillimiliax, added The Sword of Myrloch Vale to his hoard, where it remained until at least the, when the Hero of Neverwinter and their companions may have faced Icingdeath in his ghost dragon form and looted the remnants of the hoard.

## The Track

The Track was a gambling den and a tavern located on the Market Triangle in the city of Westgate in the late 14 century DR.

Interior
The entrance to The Track faced the Market Triangle. Once the visitors walked down the stairs, the entryway opened into a sizable gambling den located in a cellar. The taproom was spread around an oblong dog-racing track. Numerous tables were scattered around the hall. Beyond the gambling hall laid the establishment's kitchen, storage area, kennels, and the proprietor's offices.

Services
The Track's guests were offered betting on the dog racing, food, and a number of drinks, such as Maelstrom's Punch, Sembian Swill, Souleman's Sublime, and Brother Tobias' 1368 vintage wine.

History
In the, Thurlow Fezziwink and his cousin, Tudor Fezziwink, devised a plan to cheat at The Track's races. Thurlow concocted something he called a "simple mixture of spices" that could be smuggled past the Track's bouncers. The gnome spotted a group of well-armed adventurers on the street and chased them down to hire them for the simple task of bringing the vial of spices to Tudor, who was ready to pull the scam off from the Track's taproom to fix a race between Big Bruiser and Daleland Downs. It was unknown if the scan worked, but if it were successful, it would surely have attracted the attention of the proprietor and his shady business partners.

Inhabitants
In the late 14 century DR, The Track was fully staffed with bartenders, servers, several strict guards, one foul-tempered elvish chef, as well as a kennel master. The den's proprietor was Mordecai, who cracked a whip on visitors trying to fix the races. Under his management, all potions and magical items that could affect the race were confiscated upon entrance and only returned upon exiting The Track. Mordecai was also corrupt and squeezed coin from the gamblers and was allied with the notorious Night Masks and was protected by the Night Mask named Haman.

One of the notable guards who worked at The Track was the human named Brom.
